# Deploying the Cloudflare proof

Snapback's Cloudflare target is real but narrow. The All Aboard Contract app
has been deployed and remotely proven over Workers, a coordinator Durable
Object with SQLite, a separate V8 action isolate, same-origin static/native
assets, WebSocket Hibernation, deploy-time secrets, and demand-armed alarms.
It is a proof profile—not a general hosted Snapback product.

The target profile id is `cloudflare-do-sqlite-v8`. Read the deployed
`GET /capability` or `/inspect` result before relying on a feature; its explicit
`capabilityGaps` outrank assumptions from the local guide.

## Prove the profile locally first

Use the Node major pinned in `.node-version` (24.x) and the repository-locked
Wrangler:

```sh fragment reason="Canonical local Cloudflare regression commands, composed with the repository Node pin."
volta run --node 24.18.0 -- node cloudflare/test/local-suite.mjs
volta run --node 24.18.0 -- node cloudflare/test/measure.mjs
```

The suite inventories every non-remote gate and currently runs 28 checks.
Miniflare validates protocol, storage, handlers, secrets, egress, cron, and
hibernation-event behavior, but it cannot prove platform eviction, placement,
or billing. Those require a real Cloudflare run.

## Understand the deployed shape

One gateway Worker routes HTTP, WebSockets, capability reads, and assets to one
named app coordinator Durable Object. That object's embedded SQLite owns:

- app and system tables;
- the per-app commit-version counter;
- change journal and storage-backed subscriptions;
- connection grants and cron/config state.

A mutation commits version, rows, and journal in one `transactionSync`. Live
fan-out happens directly from that commit—there is no polling tailer. App code
is compiled into the Worker at deploy time because deployed Workers forbid
dynamic evaluation; changing schema/handlers is a redeploy, not a bundle load.

Handlers run through the stripped, single-sourced V8 harness. Queries and
mutations receive only generated `ctx` powers. Actions run in a separate
handler Worker so a slow external fetch cannot queue the coordinator's
transactional work.

## Deploy All Aboard

Deployment mutates a real Cloudflare account. Use a Workers + Durable
Objects-scoped token and an independently generated admin token; never commit
either:

```sh fragment reason="All Aboard selection added to the canonical cloudflare/README.md deployment sequence."
bun install --frozen-lockfile
export CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN=...
export CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID=...
export SNAPBACK_ADMIN_TOKEN=...
SNAPBACK_CF_APP=all-aboard ./cloudflare/deploy.sh
```

The script builds the same-origin Contract/native bundle, verifies the
repo-local Wrangler and locks, deploys handler dependencies before the gateway,
attests the exact active Worker version, and performs the final gateway deploy
after secret changes. On a partial failure it attempts to restore previously
active Worker versions; ambiguous account/API state fails closed.

An absent local `SNAPBACK_ADMIN_TOKEN` is not evidence that the remote secret
is absent. Deployment reports absent, present-and-preserved, or unknown; only
`SNAPBACK_ADMIN_TOKEN_REMOVE=1` requests attested removal.

## Configure declared secret pools

All Aboard declares `caltrainFeed` and `directions`. Send one JSON object of
non-empty string arrays over stdin, never in argv or shell history:

```sh source=cloudflare/README.md
SNAPBACK_ADMIN_TOKEN=... node cloudflare/config-set.mjs \
  --url https://snapback-all-aboard-proof.<subdomain>.workers.dev \
  --entries-stdin < /secure/path/to/secret-pools.json
```

`config-set.mjs` reads the current generation, writes changed bindings plus a
new `SNAPBACK_CONFIG_GENERATION` in one `wrangler secret bulk` activation, then
polls authenticated `/_snapback/api/config/status` (the hosted system surface
lives under `/_snapback/*`) until that generation and member counts are
attested as applied. It refuses value-bearing argv flags. Status returns
names, set/missing state, counts, and grant relationships—never values.

App actions receive descriptor handles only. Values unwrap at the coordinator's
host-fetch boundary into declared query-parameter or header slots:

```js source=cloudflare/app/all-aboard.app.js
  const response = await ctx.fetch({
    url,
    headers: { Accept: 'application/json' },
    timeoutMs: 15_000,
    secretSlots: [{ placement: 'query-param', name: 'api_key', handle }],
  });
```

Ambient `fetch`, `.expose()`, and `.asBearer()` stay unavailable in the app
isolate. The host validates HTTP(S), descriptor ownership and placement,
enforces action/fetch deadlines and bounded response bodies, and redacts secret
values before any response or diagnostic re-enters app code. This is not a
general egress claim: the two All Aboard placement shapes are proven, but a
destination allowlist is still a declared gap.

## Run the remote proof

After secrets are applied, run the real-deployment acceptance:

```sh fragment reason="All Aboard remote acceptance invocation from the runner header."
SNAPBACK_PROOF_URL=https://snapback-all-aboard-proof.<subdomain>.workers.dev \
SNAPBACK_ADMIN_TOKEN=... \
  node cloudflare/test/acceptance.remote.all-aboard.mjs
```

It proves cold start, same-origin Contract/native assets, ensure/seed, config
attestation, finite queries and mutations, real hibernating WebSocket push,
live 511/directions actions, demand-armed warm polling, eviction recovery, and
secret redaction. Expect minutes rather than seconds because it waits for a
real scheduled cycle.

For the notes proof, `cloudflare/test/acceptance.remote.mjs` additionally
records connected-idle billing windows and platform-eviction evidence. Cloudflare
analytics may settle several minutes later; re-read the emitted window before
calling observed-zero usage final.

## Hibernation, reconnect, and idle-to-zero

Server-held sockets use the Durable Object WebSocket Hibernation API. Durable
subscription rows, not isolate memory or socket attachments, are the recovery
authority. After wake/eviction, the object rehydrates them; socket loss takes a
fresh snapshot-with-subscribe. Retained-version resume and HTTP outbox delta
polling are explicit gaps.

The hosted kit socket's in-band durable surface is independently governed:
`live.kit-socket-request.schema.json` covers `subscribe`, `unsubscribe`, and
`ping`; `live.kit-socket-reply.schema.json` covers the actually served
`pong`, `snapshot`, `current_as_of`, and `error` frames. Unsubscribe is
deliberately silent. The Cloudflare wire-schema gate validates real reply bytes
against that Rust-derived contract; the older proof socket's `type`-tagged
frames are a separate pinned protocol.

The coordinator uses no always-awake interval. All Aboard's `warmPoll` is a
single Durable Object alarm dispatcher job:

- first live demand arms the alarm;
- the last unsubscribe cancels it;
- `(jobName, scheduledAt)` durable claims make alarm retry idempotent;
- an app with no subscribers schedules zero warm-poll wakeups.

Real settled evidence includes a two-hour no-demand interval with observed-zero
request/execution estimates and hibernating connected-idle measurements. This
supports the narrow proof's idle-to-zero claim; it is not a scale or price
guarantee for arbitrary apps.

## Exact supported subset and non-claims

The manifest currently claims V8, Durable Object SQLite, serialized mutation
commits, syncable/online single-table queries, replace-only live subscriptions,
the witnessed outbound-action shapes, and demand-armed cron. Enforced limits
include row/storage size, wall-clock/CPU, and subscription counts.

It explicitly does **not** claim:

- hosted authentication (only `authMode: dev` is supported);
- offline retention/replay or optimistic replay;
- ephemeral realtime rooms;
- generalized outbound actions or an egress destination allowlist;
- calendar/Cron Trigger schedules;
- R2 asset upload, notifications, Postgres, code hot-load, untrusted hosted
  tenant code, multiple apps per deployment, or a hosted marketplace;
- local pages whose `targets:` omit `cloudflare`.

See [auth target honesty](../auth/targets.md) before exposing this deployment
to users. The local bearer/dev identity posture is not production hosted auth.

## Anti-patterns

- **Do not call the proof a general Cloudflare target.** Inspect its manifest
  and keep every gap visible.
- **Do not deploy with an unlocked/ad-hoc Wrangler or `npx`.**
- **Do not pass secrets in argv, config files, logs, or app-visible errors.**
- **Do not add interval polling to keep the object warm.** Use hibernation and
  the one demand-armed alarm dispatcher.
- **Do not infer a successful local suite proves billing or eviction.** Run the
  remote evidence lane.

# Your first backend

> **Local target only.** This page describes the local dev/test target.
> Hosted targets make deliberately weaker or different claims — see
> [auth/targets](../auth/targets.md).

A Snapback backend is a directory — conventionally `<app>/snapback/` —
holding a handful of source-authored `.mjs` files plus a generated review
manifest and an ignored, regenerable artifact materialization:

For the current source/packed React path, start with
`snapback new my-app --template react`, install the generated dependencies,
and run `bun run dev`. That one script owns both this backend loop and Vite;
the exact public-versus-staged package boundary and seed-on-new-database
behavior are in [the authoring loop](./the-authoring-loop.md).

```text
myapp/
  snapback/
    schema.mjs        # source-authored schema (the source of truth)
    functions.mjs     # query/mutation/action definitions, JS handlers inline
    seed.json         # deterministic declarative seed
    generated/
      artifacts.json  # committed deterministic review manifest
      ...             # ignored cache materialization; never hand-edited
  .snapback/
    codegen-cache/    # complete graphs keyed by the complete inputsHash
```

You write the first three. Codegen owns everything under `generated/` and
`.snapback/codegen-cache/`. Commit `generated/artifacts.json` and only
consumer projections explicitly required by policy; see
[generated artifact custody](./generated-artifacts.md). (Apps on the
[legacy bundled-module form](#legacy-compatibility-bundled-handler-modules)
author one more file, `handlers.mjs`.)

## Declare the schema

All authoring helpers come from `packages/snapback-codegen/define.mjs`
(demos import it via the `demos/_kit/define.mjs` shim). A schema is tables
of validated fields, with chainable `.index(...)` and `.sync()`:

```js source=demos/todo/snapback/schema.mjs
import { defineSchema, defineTable, v } from '../../_kit/define.mjs';

export default defineSchema({
  todos: defineTable({
    title: v.string(),
    completed: v.boolean(),
    userId: v.string(),
  })
    // by_user backs the user-scoped live query's index-first lookup.
    .index('by_user', ['userId'])
    // Declared syncable so it can back the restricted syncable-live subset.
    .sync(),
});
```

The core validators: `v.string()`, `v.principal()`, `v.id(table)`,
`v.boolean()`, `v.integer()`, `v.real()` / `v.number()`, `v.json()`,
`v.object({...})`, and `v.optional(inner)`. This inventory is deliberately
partial: specialized validators — typed asset references (`v.assetRef`,
[assets](../backend/assets.md)), result-side `v.doc(table)` references
([queries](../backend/queries.md)) — are taught with their features.
`defineSchema` also takes an
options object:
`ephemeral:` (a `defineEphemeral(...)` — see the
[presence recipe](../recipes/presence-cursors.md) and complete
[ephemeral-state reference](../realtime/ephemeral-state.md)), `auth:`
(`{ mode: 'dev' | 'sessions' }` — see
[auth/sessions-and-principals](../auth/sessions-and-principals.md)), and
`requiredCapabilities:`.

The system fields `_id`, `_version`, `_createdAt`, `_updatedAt` are
server-owned. Declaring one is a hard error
(`SNAPBACK_SCHEMA_SYSTEM_FIELD`), and handlers never set timestamps.

## Define functions

There are two authoring styles, freely mixed in one `functions.mjs`:

1. **Declarative plans** (`defineQuery`, `defineLiveQuery`,
   `defineMutation`) — built from expression helpers, deterministic, no JS
   runtime involved.
2. **Inline JS handlers** (`defineJsQuery`, `defineJsLiveQuery`,
   `defineJsMutation`, `defineAction`) — one direct, self-contained
   `handler:` expression colocated with its arguments, result contract, and
   declared reads/writes, run against the injected `ctx`.

A declarative query — filter, order, index, and the server-derived user id:

```js source=demos/todo/snapback/functions.mjs
export const listTodosOnce = defineQuery({
  table: 'todos',
  args: {},
  filter: [eq('userId', authUserId())],
  order: [asc('_createdAt')],
  index: 'by_user',
});
```

A JS mutation and a JS live query in the paved inline form — each definition
carries its `handler` directly, next to `args`, `result`, and the declared
`reads`/`writes`:

```js source=packages/snapback-codegen/inline-result-contracts.test.mjs
  export const createTodo = defineJsMutation({
    args: { title: v.string() },
    writes: ['todos'],
    result: results.value(v.id('todos')),
    handler: async (ctx, args) => ctx.db.insert('todos', { title: args.title }),
  });
  export const watchTodos = defineJsLiveQuery({
    args: {},
    reads: ['todos'],
    result: results.documents('todos'),
    handler: async (ctx) => ctx.db.query('todos').collect(),
  });
```

(That excerpt is transcluded from the codegen package's inline-handler
conformance test over a minimal `todos` table, so this page breaks if the
paved form drifts. Fuller inline examples — index-first lookups, auth
scoping, multi-table writes — are transcluded from
`demos/signal-desk/snapback/functions.mjs` on the reference pages linked
below.)

A declarative mutation, for comparison:

```js source=demos/todo/snapback/functions.mjs
export const editTitle = defineMutation({
  args: { id: v.string(), title: v.string() },
  plan: patch('todos', arg('id'), { title: arg('title') }),
  returns: returnChangedCount(),
});
```

Use a declarative plan when the plan vocabulary expresses the operation; use
an inline JS handler for bounded logic it cannot express.
`demos/todo-v2/snapback/functions.mjs` is a fully declarative app, and
`demos/signal-desk/snapback/functions.mjs` mixes declarative live queries
with inline JS mutations — the side-by-sides worth reading when choosing.
The reference pages carry the complete semantics:
[queries](../backend/queries.md), [mutations](../backend/mutations.md), and
[actions](../backend/actions-and-fetch.md).

## Inside a JS handler

A handler receives only the injected `ctx` and its validated `args` — no
imports, no `process`/env, no timers, no network, no direct storage. The
core `ctx.db` surface: `ctx.db.query(table).withIndex(name).eq(field, value)`
`.in(field, [...])`.`order(field, dir)`.`collect()`, plus
`ctx.db.get(table, id)`, `ctx.db.insert(table, values)`,
`ctx.db.patch(table, id, values)`, `ctx.db.delete(table, id)`, and
`ctx.auth.userId` — the server-derived identity
([never client-asserted](../auth/sessions-and-principals.md)).

Inline v1 is deliberately self-contained: it does not capture imports,
sibling helpers, or outer constants, so put all application logic and locals
inside the direct handler expression. Class syntax, dynamic import, `eval`,
and `Function` are refused during generation.

### What the subset refuses, and the standard rewrites

Every refusal below happens at generation with a file/line/column, never at
runtime:

| Refused | Diagnostic gist | Standard rewrite |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Dynamic computed member access (`s[i]`, `vec[slot] += d`) | `dynamic computed member access is outside inline_handler_v1` | walk strings with `charAt`/`charCodeAt`; update slots with `arr.map((v, i) => i === slot ? v + d : v)` |
| Sibling capture (imports, outer consts, helper functions) | free identifier outside the allowlist | inline the logic, or declare the helper *inside* the handler body |
| An empty `writes: []` on `defineJsMutation` | `defineJsMutation requires declared writes` | declare the tables the mutation may write, even if a given path writes none |
| A query verb outside the builder | `<verb> is not a query-builder verb` | use the [documented chain](../backend/queries.md#the-complete-builder-chain) |
| Class syntax, `this`/`super`, dynamic `import`, `eval`, `Function` | named per construct | restructure as plain functions and values |

What **is** available, and needs no ceremony: `JSON.stringify`/`JSON.parse`,
`Math`, `String.fromCharCode`, template literals, arrow helpers declared
inside the handler body, ordinary array methods (`map`, `filter`, `reduce`,
`slice`, `sort`), and destructuring with static names.
[Queries](../backend/queries.md) covers the capture limits; the governing
spec is
[LLP 0108](repo:llp/0108-inline-handlers-and-result-contracts.spec.md).

Declare what a handler returns. JS query and live-query handlers return an
**array of rows** (`[]` for missing, `[row]` for present) described by
`results.documents(table)` or `results.records(v.object({...}))`; mutations
and actions use `results.value(validator)` or `results.document(table)`.
Omitting `result` is an explicit degraded `unknown` contract. The complete
result-contract vocabulary and runtime-validation rules are on
[queries](../backend/queries.md) and [mutations](../backend/mutations.md).

Membership declarations additionally generate query-side
`ctx.permissions.<declaration>` checks and mutation-only
`ctx.membership.<declaration>` operations. See
[scoped roles and memberships](../auth/scoped-roles.md) for their typed surface
and transition rules.

## Seed deterministically

```json source=demos/todo/snapback/seed.json
{
  "tables": {
    "todos": [
      { "_id": "seed_todo_1", "title": "Read the Snapback explainer", "completed": true, "userId": "user_ada" },
      { "_id": "seed_todo_2", "title": "Build the todo demo", "completed": false, "userId": "user_ada" },
      { "_id": "seed_todo_3", "title": "Write the diary", "completed": false, "userId": "user_ada" },
      { "_id": "seed_todo_4", "title": "Plan the kanban demo", "completed": false, "userId": "user_grace" }
    ]
  }
}
```

## Generate and load

```sh
node packages/snapback-codegen/index.mjs myapp/snapback
```

Codegen **fails closed**: on any error it leaves the previously serveable
graph intact and exits 1 with stable diagnostic codes
(`QUERY_UNKNOWN_FIELD`, `FUNCTION_RESERVED_EXPORT`, ...). On success it writes
a complete input-hash cache and materializes `myapp/snapback/generated/` for
compatibility — server manifests
(`schema.manifest.json`, `functions.manifest.json`), the client binding
surface (`api.mjs` + `api.d.ts`), Contract binding modules under
`contract/`, per-function argument schemas under `operations/`, and
`artifacts.json` carrying digests, custody, the `inputsHash`, and the
deterministic author summary. Commit the review manifest, not the ordinary
cache projections.

A running server loads the app over its admin API — the kit client wraps
the endpoints:

```js source=demos/todo/surfaces/headless/run.mjs
  await db.loadSchema(gen('schema.manifest.json'));
  await db.loadFunctions(gen('functions.manifest.json'));
  await db.reset();
  await db.seed(JSON.parse(readFileSync(join(backendDir, 'seed.json'), 'utf8')));
```

For a `dev`-mode app,
`db.ensureApp({ schema, functions, seed })` is the idempotent form: it
provisions only what's missing and seeds only empty tables.

Sessions-mode provisioning is deliberately explicit and admin-authorized:

```js fragment reason="generated manifests and seed come from the app build"
const db = new SnapbackClient(baseUrl, { adminToken });
await db.ensureApp({
  intent: 'provision',
  requestedMode: 'sessions',
  schema,
  functions,
  seed,
  routes,
});
```

The untagged legacy body is refused once sessions mode is active. Explicit
provisioning always carries the client's configured admin token and remains
non-production-profile gated, even when artifact hashes already match. A fresh
`dev → sessions` provision stages the sessions deployment and closes app data
until the required process restart consumes it; same-mode sessions provisioning
is idempotent without weakening the gate. Explicit mode provisioning does not
reinterpret route identity: it validates `routes` against the same candidate
schema/functions pair and installs them only with that deployment.

Then call it. Function references are the generated `api.<name>` objects
from `generated/api.mjs`, and mutations return structured results:

```js source=demos/todo/tests/acceptance/headless.mjs
    const created = await db.mutate(api.createTodo, { args: { title: 'Buy milk' }, userId: ADA });
```

Continue with [the authoring loop](./the-authoring-loop.md) for the full
edit-regenerate-test cycle, and
[testing/acceptance](../testing/acceptance.md) for the harness.

## Legacy compatibility: bundled handler modules

Before inline handlers landed, the JS style split every definition from its
logic: the definition names a bundled module and export
(`source` / `exportName`), and the logic registers on a global in a separate
authored `handlers.mjs` next to `functions.mjs`. This form remains fully
supported — `demos/todo` still uses it — but it is the compatibility lane,
not the paved path for new work.

The definition names its handler and declares its writes:

```js source=demos/todo/snapback/functions.mjs
export const createTodo = defineJsMutation({
  args: { title: v.string() },
  source: 'handlers.mjs',
  exportName: 'createTodo',
  writes: ['todos'],
});
```

The bundled module registers its logic on a global and receives the same
injected `ctx` and bounded `ctx.db` surface as an inline handler:

```js source=demos/todo/snapback/handlers.mjs
globalThis.__snapbackHandlers = {
  async listTodos(ctx) {
    return await ctx.db
      .query('todos')
      .withIndex('by_user')
      .eq('userId', ctx.auth.userId)
      .order('_createdAt', 'asc')
      .collect();
  },

  async createTodo(ctx, args) {
    const title = String(args.title ?? '').trim();
    if (!title) throw new Error('todo title is required');
    return await ctx.db.insert('todos', {
      title,
      completed: false,
      userId: ctx.auth.userId,
    });
  },
```

The `{ source, exportName }` lane reads exactly one closed script. It supports
top-level helper functions in that same file; it does not load imported helpers
or a multi-file module graph. Any static or dynamic import is refused during
generation with `BUNDLE_UNSUPPORTED_IMPORT`. Third-party package admission is
still an open code-execution and supply-chain design question, not a sanctioned
pre-bundling workaround. One definition declares `handler` or
`source`/`exportName`, never both — mixed or missing discriminants fail
generation with
`SNAPBACK_FUNCTION_HANDLER_FORM_INVALID`.

## Anti-patterns

- **Do not hand-wire HTTP glue for app data.** The generated `api.mjs`
  references plus the kit client (or the Contract adapter /
  React arm) are the product path; raw `fetch` against `/query/...` is how
  demos accumulated unauditable glue before the kit existed.
- **Do not start new JS functions on the bundled `handlers.mjs` split.**
  Inline `handler:` is the paved form; the `source`/`exportName` module lane
  is compatibility for existing apps. It is still a closed single script,
  not an import or package-admission escape hatch.
- **Do not edit anything under `generated/` or `.snapback/codegen-cache/`.**
  Regenerate. The server
  rejects stale artifacts loudly (`SNAPBACK_STALE_SCHEMA_ARTIFACT_VERSION`,
  `SNAPBACK_STALE_CONTRACT_DATA_INPUTS_HASH`).
- **Do not set `_createdAt`/`_updatedAt`/`_id`/`_version`.** Server-owned;
  declaring them in a schema is a hard error.
- **Do not assert identity from the client.** `ctx.auth.userId` is derived
  server-side; see [auth](../auth/sessions-and-principals.md).

# The authoring loop

> **Local target only.** This page describes the local dev/test target.
> Hosted targets make deliberately weaker or different claims — see
> [auth/targets](../auth/targets.md).

The cycle you repeat while building on Snapback:

```text
edit snapback/*.mjs  ->  regenerate  ->  run the acceptance suite  ->  inspect
```

The current source and packed-package React path is:

```sh
snapback doctor --json
snapback new my-app --template react
cd my-app
bun install
bun run dev
```

The generated `dev` script is one supervisor:
`snapback dev snapback --client . --client-command vite`. It generates the
backend, starts or attaches to the native server, loads the app, then starts
Vite and watches both sides. Browser code uses only Vite's relative
`/__snapback` relay; it does not receive the loopback origin, admin token,
runtime path, or repository path. The template uses generated query/mutation
references and the first-party React provider/hooks; it does not add
application-owned subscription cleanup.

The package `@expo/snapback-cli` supplies the `snapback` command — the
terminal npm identity (LLP 0115 decision 9): the workspace name and the
registry name are the same. The recorded pre-migration public closure
(`0.1.x`) was published under the interim `@ccheever/snapback-*` aliases from
the then-`@snapback/*` source names; those receipts remain verifiable as
lineage. The byte-verified public closure contains the macOS/arm64 and
Linux/x64 runtimes plus Contract, client, codegen, React, app CLI, and
developer-loop CLI packages. Clean GitHub-hosted machines on both supported
runtime tuples installed that exact closure and passed the original
`todo-contract` scaffold/generate/dev/watch proof.

The `@expo/snapback-*` **0.1.7** closure (publication ledger
`terminal-package-publication-0.1.7-fdd49db8.json`) carries the complete
public React path: `snapback new --template react`, `bun install`,
`snapback generate`, a strict typecheck, `vite build`, the `snapback dev`
lifecycle, template live acceptance with real handler execution, and a clean
stop — proven from a clean external directory by the LLP 0137 G1
qualification arm
(`demos/improvement-sweep/arms/g1-public-package-qualification/`). Treat
0.1.7 as the newest closure carrying that proof. The registry's `latest` tag
now selects the 0.1.8 closure, published 2026-08-01 as a deliberate
pre-consumer fast-path release with no qualification-arm receipt of its own
(the "Fast-path pre-consumer release" section of
[LLP 0041](repo:llp/0041-packaged-dev-loop.rfc.md)); pin `0.1.7` when you
need the proven closure.

Still do not infer that a published closure contains every surface in the
current source tree: source lands continuously, and a packaged consumer has
whatever the newest published version froze. When a page describes a surface
newer than the newest closure, it says so.

On each supported tuple the mapped runtime package carries the prebuilt server
and Hermes runtime. `doctor` first launches that relocated binary with
ambient dynamic-loader overrides removed, then creates a disposable app and
database, generates and loads its bundle, invokes a query, commits a mutation,
opens and closes a live subscription, stops the owned server through its ready
descriptor, and removes the temporary state. Its `snapback.cli-doctor.v2`
result reports one stable code per completed boundary; a launch-only result is
test instrumentation and never the installed-product claim. Other host tuples
report `SNAPBACK_IBEX_HOST_UNSUPPORTED`—they are not source-build fallbacks
disguised as installs. The former `@snapback/*` source scope belongs to an
unrelated npm product, which is why publication historically used the
`@ccheever/snapback-*` aliases; under the terminal `@expo/snapback-*` scope
application imports and published names are one identity and no alias
mapping exists.

## 1. Edit

Change `schema.mjs`, `functions.mjs`, or `seed.json`
([your first backend](./your-first-backend.md) covers each; apps on the
legacy bundled-module form also edit `handlers.mjs`).

## 2. Regenerate

In a source checkout, install the pinned workspace dependencies once before
running repository codegen:

```sh
bun install --frozen-lockfile
```

```sh
node packages/snapback-codegen/index.mjs <app>/snapback
```

Outside this repository, use the packaged equivalent:

```sh
snapback generate snapback
```

`snapback dev snapback` runs that generation first, starts or attaches to the
native server via `.snapback/dev.ready.json`, loads the generated schema and
functions, installs a generated versioned seed only for a newly created
managed database, and watches source changes through one coalesced generation
at a time. Later starts and watch reloads require the exact installed seed
identity to match; they do not reset or restore user data. A changed
`seedVersion` therefore reports `SNAPBACK_SEED_MIGRATION_REQUIRED` until you
choose migration or an explicit destructive reset-install.

The command infers `dev` versus `sessions` from the generated schema.
Sessions-mode managed starts supply the complete closed schema/functions
startup carrier before listener bind, including on backend restart; later
reloads use the complete admin-authorized provisioning pair instead of the
dev-only raw host-load verbs. The attach path validates the database target
before reading the managed owner-only token. A different target fails with
`SNAPBACK_DEV_SERVER_TARGET_MISMATCH`. If initial attach/load fails, a server
started by this command is stopped. If later generation succeeds but live load
fails, the event state is `generated-but-not-loaded`; generation errors are
the distinct `generation-failed` state.

Use `snapback --help` to enumerate the complete packaged and delegated native
surface. `snapback <command> [<subcommand>...] --help` is non-executing and
selects the longest registered wrapper path, so commands such as
`snapback backup create plan --help` show their actual required flags rather
than only the top-level backup summary. Package help also declares whether the
selected command is one-shot or long-running, its machine output, exit
taxonomy, and recovery channel. `snapback hosted lifecycle --help` lists its
closed verbs, transport flags, and current availability gate.

When `snapback dev` runs without a TTY, stdin accepts optional
`snapback.dev-command.v1` JSON lines while it remains open. EOF only closes
that control channel: it does not stop the server, watcher, or generated
client arm. Stop a detached loop with SIGINT/SIGTERM; an interactive terminal
may also use `q` or Ctrl-C. This is deliberately different from stdio MCP
servers, where EOF ends the protocol process.

If a selected native runtime predates the generated artifact shape, the loop
reports `SNAPBACK_RUNTIME_ARTIFACT_IDENTITY_MISMATCH` with the exact selected
binary, its independent build stamp when available, the artifact paths, and
two safe recovery paths: rebuild from the same source revision or point
`SNAPBACK_RUNTIME_BINARY` at a compatible binary. Do not delete generated
fields or hand-edit artifacts to fit an older runtime.

Codegen is deterministic and **fails closed** — on error it writes nothing
and exits 1 with stable diagnostic codes on stderr, so there is never
silently stale output. On success it prints an author summary and the
`inputsHash` freshness key. Commit `generated/artifacts.json` with your source
change, plus only projections explicitly named by consumer policy. The
complete graph is regenerated under `.snapback/codegen-cache/<inputsHash>/`;
see [generated artifact custody](./generated-artifacts.md). The server compares hashes and
rejects stale artifacts loudly (`SNAPBACK_STALE_SCHEMA_ARTIFACT_VERSION`,
`SNAPBACK_STALE_CONTRACT_DATA_INPUTS_HASH`) rather than serving them.

If you forget this step, the very first server load or acceptance run tells
you; nothing downstream guesses.

A raw `ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND` for `acorn`, `esbuild`, or `typescript` means the
source checkout has not completed the pinned install above. It is a contributor
environment failure, not an application diagnostic. Packaged
`snapback generate` installs these as ordinary package dependencies.

## Evolve a table that already has data

Adding an **optional** field to a populated table is an ordinary edit, not a
migration ceremony: change the schema and let the running `snapback dev`
watch reload pick it up. The reload evolves the catalog in place, and live
handles may stay attached while it happens — a subscriber does not have to be
torn down first.

What matters is *where* you do it. Stop the server, regenerate, and restart,
and a sessions-mode app refuses with
`SNAPBACK_AUTH_STARTUP_ARTIFACT_MISMATCH`, whose details carry the expected
and observed deployment identities: the settled deployment's startup carrier
no longer matches the artifacts on disk. The recovery is the running-server
path above — evolve through the watch reload rather than through a restart.

Additive changes (new optional fields, new tables, new indexes) are what this
loop supports. Destructive changes — dropping a field, tightening an optional
field to required, changing a field's type — are refused by the conservative
applier; they need the reviewed migration path
([LLP 0081](repo:llp/0081-reviewed-storage-evolution-and-migrations.rfc.md)),
not a redeploy. Seeded data is separate again: a changed seed identity reports
`SNAPBACK_SEED_MIGRATION_REQUIRED` and is resolved on the
[versioned seeds](../backend/versioned-seeds.md) page, not here.

## 3. Run the acceptance suite

Headless first — the required surface is driveable without any UI
(LLP 0012). A suite boots its own isolated server and drives the real
product path:

```sh
cd <generated-app>
npm test
```

The generated todo and React starters make that default live: it boots and
loads an isolated Snapback target, executes generated query and mutation
references, verifies loaded artifact identity, cleans up, and prints a
`snapback.starter-acceptance.v1` receipt. Use `npm run test:static` for the
faster generated-file/source-coherence check; it does not boot Snapback and
does not satisfy acceptance. Repository demos that do not use a generated
starter run their named headless suite directly, for example
`node <app>/tests/acceptance/headless.mjs`.

Exit `0` = every declared check passed; `1` = a check failed or the run was
short (zero checks can never pass); `2` = setup error. See
[testing/acceptance](../testing/acceptance.md) for the harness and server
lifecycle discipline.

For a demo in this repo, the whole-repo proof is
`scripts/verify-local-proof` (add `SNAPBACK_VERIFY_EXACT=0` for a
deliberately core-only iteration; merge CI requires the Exact-gated block).

## 4. Inspect

A running server tells you what it is actually serving:

```sh
cargo run                      # prints the admin URL on startup
curl http://127.0.0.1:4287/inspect
```

`GET /inspect` is the public projection (instance, capability facts);
`GET /_snapback/api/inspect` is the admin-gated full view, and the admin
console renders the same surface in a browser — the author's debugger for
"what schema/functions/data does this server hold right now". Structured
failures everywhere carry stable `SNAPBACK_*` diagnostic codes
(`{ code, severity, subsystem, message, details }`), so match on
`error.diagnostic.code`, never on message text.

## Anti-patterns

- **Do not hand-edit the review manifest/cache or skip the regenerate step** — the
  server's stale-artifact rejection exists because "it probably still
  matches" was wrong often enough.
- **Do not assert on diagnostic message strings.** Codes are the contract;
  messages are prose.
- **Do not point a new suite at a server you didn't start.** Suites own
  their server lifecycle; see
  [testing/acceptance](../testing/acceptance.md).
- **Do not parse server logs for readiness.** `snapback dev` consumes the
  ready-file descriptor and verifies the live target; log text is not a
  lifecycle protocol.
- **Do not set `SNAPBACK_RUNTIME_BINARY` in ordinary installed projects.** It
  is a contributor/test override. Installed apps should exercise the selected
  platform runtime package so `doctor` verifies the artifact users receive.

# Generated artifact custody and review

Codegen separates reviewable source control state from regenerable build
output. One complete input hash names one complete generated graph; every file
in that graph has a SHA-256 digest and byte count.

## Know what belongs in source control

There are exactly three custody classes:

- `review-manifest`: `snapback/generated/artifacts.json`. Commit this file. It
  is the deterministic review projection for the whole graph.
- `consumer-committed`: a projection that a source-only consumer or CI policy
  explicitly needs. Commit only the paths listed in `committedProjections` in
  `snapback/codegen.policy.json`, and add matching negations to the app's
  `.gitignore`. The closed policy record uses
  `schemaVersion: "snapback.codegen-policy.v1"`.
- `regenerable-cache`: every other generated projection. These bytes live
  under `.snapback/codegen-cache/<inputsHash>/` and are ignored.

Snapback's maintained demos, including the backend bakeoff, use this
manifest-only policy. Existing external repositories may retain a committed
legacy `generated/` tree while they migrate; that compatibility is deliberately
limited to pre-v2 manifests and explicitly declared `consumer-committed`
projections. It is not an exception for new repository-owned demos. The admin
UI's separately generated bindings remain under their existing dedicated
generator and CI gate because they are not a Snapback backend graph.

## Regenerate one complete graph

```sh
snapback generate snapback
snapback generate snapback --json
```

The human result inventories tables, operations by kind, live and ephemeral
counts, file custody, warnings, and degraded result types. A degraded result
links the authored export or schema field to the generated type and gives an
exact remediation. `--json` returns the same deterministic summary and structured
diagnostics.

Generation writes a temporary complete graph, digests it, atomically publishes
the hash-addressed cache, verifies it, then atomically materializes
`snapback/generated/` for import compatibility. A hard generation or write
failure leaves the previously serveable graph intact.

## Consume through the manifest

The packaged dev loop, runtime load, release builder, app CLI, Vite lifecycle,
Contract validation, and CI resolve generated files through `artifacts.json`.
A missing or tampered cache produces `SNAPBACK_CODEGEN_CACHE_INVALID`; run
`snapback generate snapback` to reconstruct it. Only a digest-matching
`consumer-committed` projection may be read without the cache. Codegen never
serves an unverified materialized cache projection as a stale fallback.

A release closes over the verified cache graph, not whatever files happen to
remain in `generated/`. CI regenerates from a cold cache, verifies every
digest, and diffs the review manifest plus explicitly committed consumer
projections.

Vite rewrites relative imports beneath a `generated` or
`generated-<target-profile>` directory to the verified cache file. This covers
the React/client API import and Contract's generated descriptor and
`runtime-links` imports without changing their author-friendly source spelling.
Node scripts do not have a bundler hook, so they call
`resolveGeneratedArtifact(generatedRoot, artifactPath)` before reading JSON or
dynamically importing a generated module.

## Review a codegen change

Review `artifacts.json` beside the source change. Its stable summary shows the
surface-size change, while `files` shows the content digest, logical kind,
custody, consumer, and regeneration command for every projection. Identical
inputs produce byte-identical review manifests and summaries.

If a consumer truly cannot regenerate, declare its exact projection path in
`snapback/codegen.policy.json`; do not commit the whole graph. Re-run codegen and
the review manifest will record the new custody.

## Anti-patterns

- **Do not import arbitrary files from an unverified cache path.** Resolve
  through the review manifest.
- **Do not hand-edit `generated/` or `.snapback/codegen-cache/`.** Regenerate;
  digest verification treats edits as tampering.
- **Do not add the whole generated tree to `committedProjections`.**
  Custody is a narrow consumer need, not a way to restore noisy diffs.
- **Do not fall back to stale materialized projections after a cache error.**
  Regenerate or fail closed.

---

# Secrets and deployment config

> **Local target only.** This page describes the local dev/test target.
> Hosted targets make deliberately weaker or different claims — see
> [auth/targets](../auth/targets.md).

Snapback config is deployment state, separate from app rows. Apps declare
secret entries in source; operators set values through the setup/admin
surface; only actions explicitly naming an entry in `uses` receive a
redacting handle.

## Declare names and acquisition help, never values

`defineConfig` puts public metadata in the generated function manifest:

```js source=demos/all-aboard/snapback/functions.mjs
export const appConfig = defineConfig({
  caltrainFeed: {
    description: '511.org Open Data API key',
    purpose: 'Fetches Caltrain StopMonitoring predictions for live departure boards',
    required: false,
    pool: true,
```

The v1 entry inventory is: `description`, `purpose`, `required`
(default true), `pool`, optional action `probe`, `howToGet`, and
`acquisition` metadata for the setup wizard. V1 values are secret; defaults
and non-secret values are deliberately rejected.

Values never belong in source, manifests, seed data, LLPs, or demo diaries.

## Set and inspect config

Use `/_snapback/admin/setup` for the browser wizard or the admin-gated config
API/host operations for automation. The core operations are `status`,
`set`, `unset`, and `verify`, plus the read-only `plan` dry-run.

`status` reports declaration, set state, member count, source, generation,
and verification—never value bytes:

```js source=demos/all-aboard/tests/acceptance/egress.mjs
  await suite.check('config.status reports names and states, never values', async () => {
    const { status, body, raw } = await configApi(on, 'GET', 'status');
    assertEqual(status, 200, 'status is readable');
    const entry = body.entries.find((e) => e.name === 'feedKeys');
    assert(entry, 'feedKeys is declared');
```

`set` replaces a scalar/pool or appends a pool member; `unset` removes the
deployment value. `verify` invokes the entry's declared action probe and
records only its outcome. Config survives `app.reset` because reset owns app
data, not deployment custody.

### The callable routes

The repo kit's `configApi` helper above is a thin wrapper. Consumers outside
this repository call the routes directly. Every one is admin-gated
(`x-snapback-admin-token`), and the three value-carrying writes additionally
require a loopback bind — a non-loopback plaintext bind refuses with
`SNAPBACK_CONFIG_TRANSIT_RULE`, and an SSH tunnel to the instance is the
blessed remote path.

| Operation | Request | Body |
| --- | --- | --- |
| status | `GET /_snapback/api/config/status` | — |
| plan | `GET /_snapback/api/config/plan?entry=<name>` | — |
| set | `POST /_snapback/api/config/set` | `{ "entry": "<name>", "value": "<string>" }` |
| set (pool) | `POST /_snapback/api/config/set` | `{ "entry": "<name>", "values": ["a", "b"], "append": true }` |
| unset | `POST /_snapback/api/config/unset` | `{ "entry": "<name>" }` |
| verify | `POST /_snapback/api/config/verify` | `{ "entry": "<name>" }` |

`plan` is a read-only dry-run: it reports the write locus, apply boundary,
and whether this transport would accept a value write, without writing
anything (the `entry` query parameter is optional).

Exactly one of `value` or `values` must be present: sending both, neither, or
the plausible-but-wrong `{ entry, member }` spelling refuses with
`SNAPBACK_CONFIG_VALUE_INVALID` ("provide exactly one of value or values").
Values are strings; a nested object is a deserialization error, not a config
diagnostic. `append: true` adds pool members, `append: false` (the default)
replaces the entry.

The write responses carry the new generation and set-state; they never carry
value bytes, and neither does `status`, the diagnostics ring, or any log
line. Pass values in the request body — never in argv, where a process list
would leak them.

## Read through a granted handle

An action names entries in `uses`, then reads `ctx.secrets.get(name)` for the
entry or `ctx.secrets.rotating(name)` for round-robin pool selection. Handle
stringification, interpolation, JSON, and
debug formatting redact. `.expose()` is the narrow, explicit materialization
for building an outbound request; keep the returned string local and
short-lived.

The acceptance proves accidental materialization stays redacted:

```js source=demos/all-aboard/tests/acceptance/egress.mjs
    assertEqual(config.stringified, JSON.stringify(REDACTED), 'JSON.stringify redacts');
    assertEqual(config.template, REDACTED, 'template literal redacts');
    assertEqual(config.concatenated, `prefix:${REDACTED}`, 'string concat redacts');
    assert(!config.stringified.includes('key-'), 'no key material in stringified form');
```

Queries and mutations have no `ctx.secrets`; actions cannot access an entry
outside `uses`. Missing and undeclared entries fail with stable
`SNAPBACK_CONFIG_*` diagnostics. Besides actions, the declared push seam
(`definePushSeam`) may also name entries in `uses`; that grant feeds the
engine-owned send lane, never a handler handle, and unknown names fail at
codegen with `CONFIG_USES_UNKNOWN` just as for actions.

## Anti-patterns

- **Do not put values in `defineConfig`.** It declares names and operator
  help only.
- **Do not pass secrets as function arguments or store them in app tables.**
  Use an action's granted handle.
- **Do not log or return `.expose()`.** Redaction protects the handle, not a
  copied plaintext string.
- **Do not treat `app.reset` as credential rotation.** Use `set`/`unset`
  and verification on the deployment config surface.

# Host operations

> **Local target only.** This page describes the local dev/test target.
> Hosted targets make deliberately weaker or different claims — see
> [auth/targets](../auth/targets.md).

Host operations give CLIs and agent tools one typed operating surface. The
in-process implementation and `POST /_snapback/api/host-ops` return the same
`hostOpsResult` envelope; operation variants are classified in the route
registry instead of inheriting one overly broad HTTP policy.

## Send one operation, receive one envelope

A request names `operation` plus its typed fields:

```json source=tests/host_ops_v0.rs
        json!({
            "operation": "function.run",
            "function": "createTodo",
            "args": { "title": "from host-ops" },
            "userId": "user_ada",
        }),
```

Every response contains `schemaVersion`, `resultKind: "hostOpsResult"`,
`requestId`, `operation`, `ok`, `target`, optional `authority`,
`artifacts`, `data`, `diagnostics[]`, and `next[]`. A known-but-unbuilt
operation returns `ok: false` with a structured diagnostic, never a fake 404
or empty success.

`artifacts.databaseVersion` contains an integer only when the durable cursor
decodes as an exact portable value. If storage cannot supply a trustworthy
cursor, the envelope becomes `ok: false`, serializes that value as `null`, and
carries the storage diagnostic; tooling must not substitute zero.

## Served request operations

The endpoint serves thirty request spellings:

| Request operation | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `app.inspect` | Full runtime/artifact/capability projection. |
| `app.reset` | Coordinated destructive reset, optionally with seed. |
| `app.seed.ensure.v1` | Install a generated versioned seed or observe its current match. |
| `app.seed.preview.v1` | Classify a versioned install/reset/clear without writing. |
| `app.seed.reset-install.v1` | Coordinated destructive reset plus versioned install. |
| `app.seed.clear.v1` | Coordinated destructive clear with an idempotent receipt. |
| `schema.load` | Load a generated schema manifest. |
| `functions.load` | Load a generated function/config/cron manifest. |
| `function.run` | Run a query/live query, mutation, or action with its kind-specific gate. |
| `function.explain` | Explain a supported kind; currently `mutationDryRun` is implemented. |
| `auth.mintSession` | Dev/test session mint requiring the process-bound impersonation capability. |
| `auth.rescueCollidingTable` | Operator-only pre-auth catalog collision recovery. |
| `asset.put` | Put asset bytes/metadata through the same machinery as the asset routes. |
| `asset.ensureSeedFixture` | Install or observe a deterministic seed-fixture asset. |
| `asset.inspect` | Inspect one asset record. |
| `asset.list` | List asset records. |
| `asset.retry` | Retry a failed asset processing step. |
| `asset.gcSweep` | Deterministic receipted GC sweep with an injected clock. |
| `asset.delete` | Delete one asset through the authorized deletion path. |
| `asset.rotateSigningKey` | Rotate the delivery signing key, invalidating outstanding signed URLs. |
| `asset.exportCut` | Export a consistent asset cut to an absolute directory. |
| `asset.importCut` | Import a previously exported consistent asset cut. |
| `telemetry.stats` | Aggregated telemetry statistics (structural metadata). |
| `telemetry.events` | Bounded filtered raw telemetry events (secret-read lease). |
| `telemetry.export` | Bounded NDJSON telemetry export (secret-read lease). |
| `errors.issues` | Structural error-issue listing. |
| `errors.issue` | Raw detail for one error issue (secret-read lease). |
| `errors.transition` | Resolve/ignore state transition for one issue. |
| `debug.networkProfileGet` | Return the active network condition profile and its activation provenance. |
| `debug.networkProfileSet` | Activate a built-in named profile or an inline profile through the shared activation gate. |

`host.start` and `host.stop` are CLI-only lifecycle verbs today—a running
server cannot safely own starting/stopping itself; over HTTP they fail as
`SNAPBACK_HOST_OP_CLI_ONLY`, and the `snapback` CLI is their working
projection. `host.restart` also fails as `SNAPBACK_HOST_OP_CLI_ONLY` over
HTTP, but has no CLI command yet; its only current projection is the
composed `snapback_restart` MCP tool, which spawns `host.stop` then
`host.start` under one request id and envelope (a `snapback restart` CLI
command is planned but not shipped).
`schema.reload`, `functions.reload`, and `acceptance.run` are pinned but
unbuilt and fail as `SNAPBACK_HOST_OP_UNIMPLEMENTED`. All three families are
registered at AdminWrite so an authenticated request reaches that structured
envelope; unknown names stay unregistered and fail closed before dispatch.

## The exact 41 registry identities

The HTTP request names above expand into these 41 audited operation
identities (the last six are the registered CLI-only and pinned-unbuilt
verbs):

1. `host_ops.app.inspect`
2. `host_ops.function.explain`
3. `host_ops.function.explain.impersonated`
4. `host_ops.app.reset`
5. `host_ops.app.seed.ensure.v1`
6. `host_ops.app.seed.preview.v1`
7. `host_ops.app.seed.reset-install.v1`
8. `host_ops.app.seed.clear.v1`
9. `host_ops.schema.load`
10. `host_ops.functions.load`
11. `host_ops.auth.mintSession`
12. `host_ops.auth.rescueCollidingTable`
13. `host_ops.function.run.query`
14. `host_ops.function.run.mutation`
15. `host_ops.function.run.action`
16. `host_ops.function.run.unknown`
17. `host_ops.function.run.impersonated`
18. `host_ops.asset.put`
19. `host_ops.asset.ensureSeedFixture`
20. `host_ops.asset.inspect`
21. `host_ops.asset.list`
22. `host_ops.asset.retry`
23. `host_ops.asset.gcSweep`
24. `host_ops.asset.delete`
25. `host_ops.asset.rotateSigningKey`
26. `host_ops.asset.exportCut`
27. `host_ops.asset.importCut`
28. `host_ops.telemetry.stats`
29. `host_ops.telemetry.events`
30. `host_ops.telemetry.export`
31. `host_ops.errors.issues`
32. `host_ops.errors.issue`
33. `host_ops.errors.transition`
34. `host_ops.debug.networkProfileGet`
35. `host_ops.debug.networkProfileSet`
36. `host_ops.schema.reload`
37. `host_ops.functions.reload`
38. `host_ops.acceptance.run`
39. `host_ops.host.start`
40. `host_ops.host.stop`
41. `host_ops.host.restart`

Query/explain reads, durable writes, credential-producing operations, and
dev impersonation therefore keep distinct `RoutePolicy`, authority, effect,
and response-sensitivity classifications even though they share one carrier.

## Respect admin, secret-read, and impersonation gates

The admin credential authenticates the transport; it does not silently invent
an app caller. In sessions mode, sensitive query/explain results additionally
require the bounded admin-secret-read lease. An impersonated branch requires
the process-bound capability and is unavailable in production. Destructive
reset, versioned reset-install, and versioned clear run through the same
authorization-stream coordinator and fail closed if that projection is
unavailable. Every `app.seed.*.v1` operation is AdminWrite + NonProd,
including preview. Its Rust-owned body belongs only under `input`; legacy
`seed`/`schema`/`functions` siblings are refused.

The partial local `servicePrincipal`/scoped-token slice is admitted only by
generated app-data calls. Host operations—including `function.run`—do not
resolve scoped tokens into authority; use the operation's explicit admin or
dev-impersonation gate instead.

## Anti-patterns

- **Do not call internal Rust methods from tooling.** Use the envelope so CLI
  and HTTP behavior stay identical.
- **Do not treat all host ops as AdminWrite.** The registry's kind-specific
  policy is part of the security boundary.
- **Do not interpret an unimplemented diagnostic as an absent operation.**
  Pinned future verbs fail explicitly.
- **Do not place credentials in request ids, logs, or `next[]`.** Credential
  operations use their dedicated response-sensitivity path.

# Network condition profiles

> **Local target only.** This page describes the local dev/test target.
> Hosted targets make deliberately weaker or different claims — see
> [auth/targets](../auth/targets.md).

Use a network condition profile when you need real Snapback responses to arrive
slowly while commits and server-side ordering remain unchanged. The delay is
applied on the server's mutation-ack, live-delta, and query-response egress
lanes, so optimistic UI, settlement, and convergence experience the same
conditions an actual client would.

## Choose a built-in or custom profile

Snapback ships three built-ins:

| Profile | Mutation ack | Live delta | Query response | Jitter | Use it for |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| `normal` | 0 ms | 0 ms | 0 ms | 0 ms | Ordinary operation; the identity profile. |
| `optimistic` | 1,000 ms | 1,000 ms | 0 ms | 0 ms | Exercising optimistic UI and coordinated post-commit settlement. |
| `demo-slow` | 2,000 ms | 2,000 ms | 2,000 ms | 250 ms | Making slow-server behavior visible in a demo. |

Anywhere a built-in name is accepted, you may instead supply an inline JSON
object with a name and the three lane delays. `jitterMs` is optional and
defaults to zero. This is the real `demo-slow` shape from the zero-bakeoff
acceptance environment:

```json source=demos/zero-bakeoff/protocol/environment.v2.json
{
      "name": "demo-slow",
      "mutationAckDelayMs": 2000,
      "liveDeltaDelayMs": 2000,
      "queryResponseDelayMs": 2000,
      "jitterMs": 250
    }
```

## Set or inspect a profile from the CLI

Address the running server through its readiness file. `get` is read-only;
`set` uses the ordinary admin-write authority and returns the structured
`hostOpsResult` envelope.

```sh
snapback network-profile get --ready-file .snapback/dev.ready.json
snapback network-profile set optimistic --ready-file .snapback/dev.ready.json
snapback network-profile set demo-slow --ready-file .snapback/dev.ready.json
```

Pass custom JSON as the positional profile value:

```sh
snapback network-profile set '{"name":"ack-slow","mutationAckDelayMs":1500,"liveDeltaDelayMs":0,"queryResponseDelayMs":0,"jitterMs":0}' --ready-file .snapback/dev.ready.json
```

## Give an agent the same control through MCP

The tools are exposed by `snapback mcp-control` and call the same host
operations as the CLI:

| Intent | MCP tool | Input |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Read the active profile and provenance | `snapback_network_profile_get` | No input. |
| Activate a profile | `snapback_network_profile_set` | `profile` is a built-in name or the inline object above; `operatorPrincipal` is optional. |

The underlying operations are `debug.networkProfileGet` and
`debug.networkProfileSet`. The latter is mutating even though a profile does
not change durable app data. Use `snapback_network_profile_set` with
`profile: "normal"` as the MCP restore step.

## Select a profile at server startup

Set `SNAPBACK_NETWORK_PROFILE` to a built-in name or inline JSON before the
server starts:

```sh
SNAPBACK_NETWORK_PROFILE=optimistic \
  snapback start --memory --ready-file .snapback/dev.ready.json
```

This is startup configuration. Restarting with the same environment selects
the profile again, and a non-`normal` selection is re-announced in startup and
readiness output. Startup selection still passes through the same activation
gate as every runtime control.

## Read or change the profile through the admin API

The admin API exposes one path with policy split by method:

| Request | Authority | Body |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GET /_snapback/api/debug/network-profile` | `AdminRead` | None. |
| `PUT /_snapback/api/debug/network-profile` | `AdminWrite` | A JSON built-in name such as `"optimistic"`, or the inline profile object. |

For example, after resolving the server URL and admin token from the readiness
handoff:

```sh
curl -sS \
  -H "x-snapback-admin-token: $ADMIN_TOKEN" \
  http://127.0.0.1:4287/_snapback/api/debug/network-profile

curl -sS -X PUT \
  -H "x-snapback-admin-token: $ADMIN_TOKEN" \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  --data '"demo-slow"' \
  http://127.0.0.1:4287/_snapback/api/debug/network-profile
```

The response reports the active profile and activation provenance. Do not
build a separate policy path around these routes; the CLI, host-ops, MCP, and
console are thin clients over the same activation decision.

## Toggle a profile while debugging in the console

The admin console's Developer panel offers all three built-ins plus custom
fields. While any non-`normal` profile is active, the console shows a
persistent banner on every tab. The panel inherits the same refusal and
authority behavior as the API; it does not have a browser-only bypass.

## Know where activation is allowed

Network profiles fail closed at one activation chokepoint. The complete matrix
and rationale live in [LLP 0167](repo:llp/0167-network-condition-profiles.rfc.md),
but these limits matter when operating the feature:

- A local, non-`Prod` server may activate a non-`normal` profile.
- A primary hosted target refuses every non-`normal` profile. The narrow
  hosted exception is an LLP 0158 derived/forked instance with authoritative,
  boot-validated identity. On Cloudflare that identity comes from the dedicated
  `SNAPBACK_DERIVED_INSTANCE_ID` binding, independently of `SNAPBACK_TESTING`.
- An explicit or defaulted `ServerProfile` of `Prod` always refuses a
  non-`normal` profile, including on a derived instance.
- Hosted, missing, malformed, or contradictory classification refusals use
  `SNAPBACK_NETWORK_PROFILE_FORBIDDEN` on every activation surface.
- The hard per-response delay ceiling is 30,000 ms. A profile that could
  exceed it is refused with `SNAPBACK_NETWORK_PROFILE_DELAY_CEILING`; Snapback
  never silently clamps it.

These rules are why this page declares `targets: [local]`: the derived-instance
allowance is a contained exception, not general hosted or production support.

## Tell whether a response was perturbed

Every response served under a non-`normal` profile names the profile that
actually governed its delay:

| Surface | Observation marker |
| --- | --- |
| HTTP | `snapback-network-profile` response header, exposed through CORS. |
| Socket and poll live protocol | `network_profile` field on the frame. |

The profile is snapshotted when the response or frame enters the delay seam, so
a concurrent toggle cannot relabel an in-flight response. `normal` is a true
identity: it emits no marker and adds no measurable overhead.

## Understand what survives a restart

A profile selected at runtime through the API, host-ops, MCP, or console is
deliberately process-local and is not persisted. After restart, the server uses
`normal` unless `SNAPBACK_NETWORK_PROFILE` supplies startup configuration.
This prevents a forgotten interactive toggle from silently becoming durable;
an environment-selected profile is different because the launcher explicitly
selects it again at startup.

## Restore `normal` when you're done

Restoring the identity profile is mandatory cleanup for every test, demo, or
debugging session that activates a non-`normal` profile. It is part of the
honest-perturbation contract in LLP 0167, not an optional courtesy:

```sh
snapback network-profile set normal --ready-file .snapback/dev.ready.json
```

If the profile came from `SNAPBACK_NETWORK_PROFILE`, also remove that setting
from the launcher or change it to `normal`; otherwise the next restart will
select the non-`normal` profile again.

The exact MCP equivalent is `snapback_network_profile_set` with
`profile: "normal"`. Confirm with the CLI `get` command or
`snapback_network_profile_get` before handing the server to another task.

## Anti-patterns

- **Do not leave a slow profile active.** Always perform and verify the
  restore-to-`normal` step above, even when a test fails midway.
- **Do not add client-side sleeps to simulate server latency.** Latency
  Kanban's old sleep delayed the caller without exercising Snapback's pending,
  settlement, and live-convergence paths; the server profile exists to replace
  that false test.
- **Do not assume hosted or production accepts non-`normal`.** Primary hosted
  and every `Prod` profile refuse it; the derived-instance rule is the only
  narrow hosted exception.
- **Do not use latency profiles to model disconnects, drops, reordering, or
  offline state.** Profiles delay otherwise unchanged, in-order observations;
  those other perturbations belong to their dedicated test controls.

---

# Diagnostics and local doctoring

Snapback failures carry stable machine identity. Assert and branch on the
`SNAPBACK_*` code; display the message to a human; inspect `details` only
for code-specific facts.

The same contract applies before runtime. Compiler, codegen, dev-server, and
surface-construction failures must carry a stable code, point at the authored
offender (file plus span when known), preserve the first actionable cause, and
report once per source/artifact generation—not once per reactive evaluation.
An authoring failure that can be known during codegen or boot must not be
deferred into an error-shaped data cell.

## Consume the diagnostic shape

The full diagnostic is:

- `code`: stable machine classification;
- `severity`: lowercase `info | warning | error | fatal`;
- `subsystem`: stable owning subsystem;
- `message`: human explanation, not an API;
- `details`: structured code-specific context.

Public unauthenticated projections intentionally drop `message` and
`details`, because they can contain source paths, handler text, arguments, or
operator context. Error envelopes expose the diagnostic at
`error.diagnostic`; some terminal mutation paths also attach a receipt.

## Assert on codes, not prose

The shared acceptance helper demonstrates the rule:

```js source=demos/_kit/harness.mjs
export async function assertThrows(fn, code, message) {
  try {
    await fn();
  } catch (error) {
    const got = error.diagnostic?.code ?? error.message;
    if (code && got !== code) throw new Error(`${message ?? 'wrong error'}: expected ${code}, got ${got}`);
    return error;
  }
  throw new Error(`${message ?? 'expected an error'}: nothing thrown (wanted ${code})`);
}
```

Messages may improve without a compatibility event. A code change is a
contract change and must update its schemas, callers, tests, and docs together.

A native `snapback start` without `--ready-file` may hand process-bound
capabilities to a controlling terminal. A detached start has no safe carrier
and fails before database creation with
`SNAPBACK_READY_DESCRIPTOR_REQUIRED`; its diagnostic `details.next` names
`snapback start --ready-file <owner-only-path> ...` as the repair. Never scrape
the human startup log or redirect a bearer through inherited stdout/stderr.

## Repair ambient time and identifier diagnostics

During handler generation, `BUNDLE_UNSUPPORTED_TIME`,
`BUNDLE_UNSUPPORTED_RANDOM`, and `BUNDLE_UNSUPPORTED_TIMER` include a
suggested repair and route to
[trusted runtime time and identifiers](../backend/trusted-runtime-values.md).
Use `ctx.runtime.now()` for a trusted integer timestamp and
`ctx.runtime.id()` for a fresh identifier. Neither method is a general
replacement for randomness, delay, or scheduling.

## Diagnose the vendored Ibex runtime first

Run the read-only doctor before repairing runtime files by hand:

```sh
scripts/ibex-doctor
```

It checks the submodule state, prepared Hermes artifacts/framework, CLI,
required tools, and then the part file-presence checks cannot prove: an exact
link of this checkout's final `snapback` Cargo target in an automatically
cleaned temporary target directory, followed by launch and restricted
handler-VM qualification of that newly linked binary with `DYLD_*` and
`LD_LIBRARY_PATH` scrubbed. It also verifies, read-only, that the served
binary's persisted readiness receipt (`<binary>.runtime-readiness.json`) is
digest-coherent with that binary and the current Hermes artifacts. An older
runnable binary does not make the current checkout green. On a clean checkout, bootstrap before
Cargo build/test/run:

```sh
scripts/bootstrap-ibex-runtime
```

Bootstrap distinguishes a structurally complete Hermes set from one compatible
with the vendored Ibex revision. Before using installed artifacts or copying a
prepared checkout, it reconstructs the vendored authority-bound source-cache
keys and requires the artifact receipt to match. An incompatible `../ibex` (or
`SNAPBACK_IBEX_CHECKOUT`) is skipped for the vendored download/build fallback;
Ibex `build.rs` still performs the authoritative full-identity validation. Do
not copy a receipt or edit its identity by hand.

The stable bootstrap failure vocabulary is:
`SNAPBACK_IBEX_SOURCE_MISSING`,
`SNAPBACK_IBEX_SUBMODULE_BROKEN`,
`SNAPBACK_IBEX_SUBMODULE_INIT_FAILED`,
`SNAPBACK_IBEX_SUBMODULE_WEDGED`,
`SNAPBACK_CAPABILITY_IBEX_HERMES_MISSING`,
`SNAPBACK_IBEX_HERMES_DOWNLOAD_FAILED`,
`SNAPBACK_IBEX_CARGO_BUILD_FAILED`,
`SNAPBACK_IBEX_RUNTIME_LINK_FAILED`,
`SNAPBACK_IBEX_RUNTIME_LINK_TIMEOUT`,
`SNAPBACK_IBEX_RUNTIME_LINK_INTERRUPTED`,
`SNAPBACK_IBEX_RUNTIME_LINK_PROBE_FAILED`,
`SNAPBACK_IBEX_RUNTIME_LOAD_FAILED`,
`SNAPBACK_IBEX_RUNTIME_VM_CREATE_FAILED`,
`SNAPBACK_IBEX_RUNTIME_RECEIPT_INVALID`, and
`SNAPBACK_IBEX_HOST_UNSUPPORTED`.

The doctor additionally distinguishes uninitialized/conflicting/drifted
submodules, a missing vendored CLI, missing Node/Bun/Cargo, and dynamic-loader
configuration. Follow the emitted next checks; do not collapse those states
into “build failed.”

Every runtime entry point exposes the same
`snapback.runtime-recovery.v1` record: repository doctor (`runtimeRecovery` in
`--json`), bootstrap (one `runtime recovery record:` line), packaged
`snapback doctor` and `snapback dev` (`runtimeRecovery`), and demo
`startServer` (`handle.runtimeRecovery`, or `error.runtimeRecovery` on launch
failure). It names the selected binary and resolver rung, expected checkout
commit/dirty state, actual build stamp, whether the current checkout proved
buildable/runnable, why automatic reuse was allowed or refused, exact producer
inputs, and safe repair or explicit override.

The read-only native `snapback build-identity` command prints
`snapback.binary-identity.v1` without binding a port. Doctor and helpers use it
to obtain the executable's independently embedded commit, dirty state, crate
version, and build profile; older binaries that predate the command may still
be classified runnable via `--help`, but their actual stamp remains honestly
unknown.

A dirty worktree triggers the same posture at server spawn: the kit skips
a prebuilt `target/debug/snapback` it cannot verify against a committed
identity ("this checkout is dirty or has no committed identity") and
falls back to the `cargo run` rung, which costs a rebuild-check on every
boot (~30 s). That is provenance working as designed, not a fault. If
you accept the local binary knowingly — a test loop on an intentionally
dirty tree — the sanctioned escape is the same explicit override the
diagnostic quotes: `SNAPBACK_SERVER_BINARY=<path>`. The override's
unpinned identity stays visible in the spawn record, so acceptance is
always a recorded choice, never an ambient default.

When `SNAPBACK_IBEX_RUNTIME_LINK_FAILED` names compatibility symbols such as
`ex_hermes_create_no_eval`, do not delete Cargo output or rebuild Hermes
blindly. Run the recorded bootstrap command. If the record also names a
runnable stale binary, use its quoted `SNAPBACK_SERVER_BINARY=...` override
only as an explicit temporary escape; its independent stamp and resolver rung
remain visible, so the override cannot masquerade as a current-checkout build.

For an installed application runtime, run the packaged vertical-slice doctor:

```sh
snapback doctor --json
```

It emits `snapback.cli-doctor.v2` and succeeds only after
`SNAPBACK_RUNTIME_LAUNCH_OK`, `SNAPBACK_DOCTOR_BUNDLE_LOAD_OK`,
`SNAPBACK_DOCTOR_QUERY_OK`, `SNAPBACK_DOCTOR_MUTATION_OK`,
`SNAPBACK_DOCTOR_LIVE_OK`, and `SNAPBACK_DOCTOR_SHUTDOWN_OK`. The probe uses a
fresh temporary database and an owned ready descriptor. A path mismatch,
failed load, malformed query result, non-committing mutation, missing live row,
shutdown failure, or cleanup failure remains the first structured error and
cannot be converted into a green file-presence check.

## Report the runtime's own readiness identity

`doctor` proves the whole loop. When you want just the runtime's identity —
"which binary is this, and does its handler VM come up in the restricted
no-eval posture?" — ask the binary directly:

```sh
snapback runtime-qualify
```

It prints a `snapback.runtime-qualify.v1` result carrying the VM profile
(`restricted-no-eval-handler-vm`), `ok`, and the binary's build stamp. It
creates the same VM every JS handler uses, so a mismatched Hermes framework
or a runtime/glue contract skew fails here rather than at the first handler
invocation. This is the identity to quote in a bug report or a packaged
consumer's readiness note.

Persist the live verdict and its binary/Hermes digests in the app's managed
state, then re-verify it later without writing or launching the runtime:

```sh
snapback runtime-qualify --persist
snapback runtime-qualify --verify
```

The first command still performs the restricted-VM qualification and writes
`.snapback/runtime-readiness.json`; the second recomputes the installed
runtime bytes and refuses binary or framework drift. Use `--receipt <path>`
on both commands only when another app-owned custody path is required. The
receipt uses the same `snapback.runtime-readiness.v1` schema as the repo-side
bootstrap proof ([LLP 0010](repo:llp/0010-agent-dx-and-acceptance.spec.md))
but never writes into read-only `node_modules`. Doctor's live six-boundary
qualification stays authoritative — this retained identity complements it,
never replaces it.

## Preserve the first useful failure

Acceptance harnesses must fail during setup instead of reporting a vacuous
0/0 pass, bound every wait, include the diagnostic body when an assertion
fails, and clean up their server/handles. When one failure cascades, fix and
rerun from the earliest stable code rather than patching later symptoms.

## Anti-patterns

- **Do not parse `message` text.** Use `diagnostic.code` and typed details.
- **Do not expose full diagnostics on public endpoints.** Use the public
  classification projection.
- **Do not rebuild Hermes first.** Doctor, then let bootstrap select compatible
  prepared artifacts or the vendored fallback.
- **Do not accept a zero-check or timeout-only test result.** Require the
intended diagnostic and non-vacuous witnesses.

Two early data-seam examples are intentionally blocking:

- `FUNCTION_JS_QUERY_STATIC_RESULT_NOT_ROWS` rejects a JavaScript query whose
  handler visibly returns an object literal; return `[row]` or `[]`. Dynamic
  result shapes still meet the runtime rows-array guard.
- `SNAPBACK_CONTRACT_QUERY_UNCONFIGURED` rejects a mounted component's
  `requiredQueries` before the multi-live surface opens any subscription.
