# Admin console

> **Local target only.** This page describes the local dev/test target.
> Hosted targets make deliberately weaker or different claims — see
> [auth/targets](../auth/targets.md).

The admin console is Snapback's browser debugger over
`/_snapback/api/*`. Its Contract app exposes Overview, Health, Errors, Logs,
Schema, Data, Functions, Secrets, Capabilities, Realtime, and Diagnostics views
from the same inspect/scan/runner/config boundaries used by tests and tools. Its Docs tab
renders the build-matched served guide from the generated manifest; the
console's text renderer never injects guide HTML.

## Launch the built console

Build the static browser and native Exact artifacts, then start Snapback:

```sh
cd admin-ui
./build.sh
cargo run --manifest-path ../Cargo.toml -- --memory
```

The server serves the immutable `dist/` snapshot at
`/_snapback/admin/`. Set `SNAPBACK_ADMIN_DIST` to pin another snapshot; in
a checkout, an unset value discovers `admin-ui/dist` when it exists. If no
dist is available, the route returns a structured missing-dist diagnostic
instead of a second embedded implementation.

Browser baseline:

```sh
cargo run -- --memory --ready-file .snapback/dev.ready.json
# in another terminal: discover the token, mint a browser credential, and open
cargo run -- admin --ready-file .snapback/dev.ready.json
```

For a headless machine, print the URL instead:

```sh
cargo run -- admin --ready-file .snapback/dev.ready.json --no-open
```

The URL carries only a derived `sbcc_` credential and its expiry in the
fragment. It never carries the `sbat_` master token in either the query or the
fragment. The page removes the fragment before boot and stores the derived
record through the same `snapback_console_credential_v1` path used by the paste
fallback.

For a native Exact shell, point `EXACT_APP_CUSTOM_URL` at the
Snapback-served static admin URL. A browser-only dist returns a specific
native-artifact capability diagnostic.

## Use the browser development loop

Run Snapback at a known port, then start the Exact/Contract Vite app:

```sh
cargo run -- --memory --port 4287
SNAPBACK_ADMIN_DEV_API=http://127.0.0.1:4287 bun run --cwd admin-ui dev
```

The dev server regenerates Contract bindings, watches their inputs, and proxies
`/_snapback/api/*` to the configured backend. It binds loopback by default.
Non-loopback proxy exposure requires both
`SNAPBACK_ADMIN_DEV_HOST` and
`SNAPBACK_ADMIN_DEV_ALLOW_NON_LOOPBACK=1`; treat that as exposing a
privileged operator surface.

If the backend is down, the proxy returns
`SNAPBACK_ADMIN_DEV_API_UNREACHABLE` rather than HTML or a blank app.
Static native artifacts remain build-only; request them from the served
`./build.sh` output, not the dev server.

## Authenticate the operator surface

Loopback reads are open until an admin token exists; writes and non-loopback
access follow the server's admin policy. Use the printed/token-file credential,
never app session credentials. Sessions-mode sensitive reads use a separate
short-lived admin-secret-read lease; neither credential substitutes for the
other.

The UI clears submitted credentials and renders hostile diagnostics as text:

```js source=admin-ui/tests/fatal-rendering.mjs
assert.equal(root.children[0].tagName, 'pre');
assert.equal(
  root.children[0].textContent,
  `Admin console failed to start:\n${hostile}`,
);
assert.equal('innerHTML' in root.children[0], false);
```

The production browser proof also enforces CSP hashes, Trusted Types, zero
runtime exceptions, zero console errors, and zero policy violations.

Active dev/loopback console credentials renew on a ten-minute sliding window,
up to eight hours from first mint. File-backed servers atomically persist only
the expiring SHA-256 digest metadata beside the database, so a restart does not
log out a live console. The master token remains in its separate owner-only
capability file and never enters browser storage or the digest store.

For a remote browser reached through SSH or another loopback-preserving tunnel,
the token prompt also displays a short-lived user code. Approve it from a
terminal with ready-file access:

```sh
cargo run -- admin approve ABCD-1234 --ready-file .snapback/dev.ready.json
```

The browser polls for its derived credential. Codes expire after ten minutes,
are single-use, and the request, approval, poll, and pending-state lanes are
bounded. Non-loopback binds, hosted targets, and non-dev profiles cannot use
this flow.

### Hand a one-time link from an agent terminal to a remote browser

When the token-holding terminal is remote or agent-driven, keep Snapback bound
to loopback and forward the console origin through SSH or another tunnel. Mint
the browser handoff from the trusted ready file, substituting only the tunnel's
public origin in the printed link:

```sh
cargo run -- admin link \
  --ready-file .snapback/dev.ready.json \
  --url-base https://snapback-console.example
```

The command prints
`https://snapback-console.example/_snapback/admin/#claim=sbcl_…` and stays
attached by default. Opening it removes the fragment before boot, sends the
claim only in a `POST` body, and stores the resulting `sbcc_` credential through
the ordinary console-credential path. Exactly one exchange wins. The link is a
bearer until its thirty-minute claim expiry, so keep it private while pending;
after redemption or expiry it is inert and may safely remain in agent
transcripts or scrollback. The master `sbat_` token must never enter those
channels.

The attached command reports redemption time and the direct transport peer.
Behind a tunnel that address is usually the tunnel endpoint, not the human's
browser. For detached automation, print and exit, then reattach or revoke with
the raw claim code:

```sh
cargo run -- admin link --no-wait --ready-file .snapback/dev.ready.json
cargo run -- admin link --status sbcl_… --ready-file .snapback/dev.ready.json
cargo run -- admin link --revoke sbcl_… --ready-file .snapback/dev.ready.json
```

Claim-derived credentials have distinct provenance. Active use renews their
ten-minute sliding expiry, but the server fixes their absolute deadline at
ninety minutes from redemption rather than the ordinary eight-hour ceiling.
Status and revocation require the master bearer; neither the browser nor an
anonymous loopback caller can read the redemption record. Claim mint and
exchange refuse hosted or non-loopback targets even when another admin bearer
is present—remote access is always a tunnel terminating on loopback plus
`--url-base`.

### Open a phone console on the local network

Keep the Snapback server on loopback and let the attached command own a
short-lived relay on the one eligible physical LAN interface:

```sh
cargo run -- admin link --lan --qr \
  --ready-file .snapback/dev.ready.json
```

If more than one interface is eligible, the command refuses and lists the
candidates. Select one explicitly with `--lan=en0` or
`--lan=192.168.1.20`; wildcard and loopback addresses are refused. The first
line and the terminal QR encode the same URL bytes. Scan it while the command
remains attached.

The relay is deliberately plain HTTP. Read the mint-time warning: another
party on that network can observe or hijack the session while it is live. The
compensating bounds are the single-use claim, ten-minute sliding credential
expiry, ninety-minute absolute cap, redemption record, and master revocation.
Use the tailnet recipe below on a network you do not trust.

Only the console shell/assets, the claim exchange, and requests already
carrying the derived console credential cross this relay. It refuses the
master exchange, the master-token header, non-console paths, ambiguous HTTP
framing, and hostile Host/Origin values. Closing the command, revoking the
claim, losing the observed server, or reaching claim/credential expiry closes
the listener. `--lan` therefore cannot be combined with `--no-wait`.

### Open the console across a tailnet

With tailscaled running and the target server on `127.0.0.1`, publish only the
Snapback namespace through tailnet-terminated HTTPS:

```sh
cargo run -- admin link --tailscale --qr \
  --ready-file .snapback/dev.ready.json
```

The command creates or shares a Tailscale Serve mapping only for
`/_snapback`, records its exact mapping and live owners in owner-only receipt
files, and removes it when the last attached invocation exits. A later
invocation sweeps a receipt-owned mapping stranded by a crash. Existing or
externally changed operator mappings are refused and never removed. A missing
or stopped tailscaled is a stable refusal; there is no LAN or loopback
fallback. Like `--lan`, this mode cannot be detached with `--no-wait`.

Credentials redeemed through either managed origin are stored only in the
current tab's `sessionStorage`, keyed by reachability session and server
startup identity. Reload first verifies both identities without sending the
credential. Expiry, revocation, origin reuse by another backend, or early
front termination clears or invalidates the record; it never falls back to
`localStorage` on the relay or tailnet origin.

## Debug through declared views

- **Overview/Capabilities/Realtime/Diagnostics:** inspect target, artifacts,
  capability gaps, delivery state, receipts, and stable codes.
- **Health:** telemetry stat tiles, requests over time, per-route/function
  latency, top volume/error-rate entries, lifecycle markers, and coverage,
  with a link into Errors when issues need attention.
- **Errors:** triage open/regressed issues and resolve or ignore them;
  structural metadata is ordinary admin authority, while raw detail spends a
  scoped `errors.issue` secret-read lease.
- **Logs:** filter the same bounded `telemetry.events` operation agents use;
  raw rows require a `telemetry.events` secret-read lease.
- **Schema/Data:** inspect declared tables and page through rows; private reads
  remain subject to secret-read scope/budgets.
- **Functions:** run queries, mutations, and actions through the classified
  direct-runner boundary and inspect captured reads/writes.
- **Secrets:** see declaration/set/verification state and run declared probes;
  values never render.
- **Docs:** navigate the same manifest/corpus served at `/_snapback/guide`,
  with response hash/build identity checked before a page renders.

Use the [host operations](./host-ops.md) page for automation and
[diagnostics](./diagnostics.md) for code-driven troubleshooting.

## Verify the Contract/Exact seam

The build preset owns plugin ordering, route/entry preflight, static/native
targets, and the admin base-path rewrite. Snapback's Exact discovery/conformance
helpers remain optional for ordinary core work:

```sh
node packages/snapback-contract/exact-conformance.mjs
node packages/snapback-contract/exact-conformance.mjs --require
node packages/snapback-contract/exact-conformance.mjs --run
```

`--require` makes a lane fail unless Exact registers the provider suite;
`--run` invokes Exact's registered check. Generated descriptor/project
semantics are covered by the Contract adapter acceptance, not by a hand-written
admin binding layer.

## Anti-patterns

- **Do not run the privileged dev proxy on a LAN accidentally.**
- **Do not point a native shell at a browser Vite surface.** Use the built
  Snapback-served admin URL.
- **Do not persist admin or secret-read credentials in UI state/storage.**
- **Do not put the `sbat_` master token in any URL.** The CLI fragment handoff
  is for derived `sbcc_` credentials only.
- **Do not bypass generated Contract bindings with a second admin UI.**

# Backend observability

> **Local target only.** This page describes the local dev/test target.
> Hosted targets make deliberately weaker or different claims — see
> [auth/targets](../auth/targets.md).

Snapback records a bounded, loss-tolerant recent history of backend work with
no application setup. Use the fixed Health and Logs console pages for a quick
view; use the typed operations below when an agent needs exact filters,
coverage facts, or an export.

The local implementation, recurring smoke gate, and retained clean-release
idle/benchmark receipt are shipped together. The
[retained carrier](repo:tests/acceptance/telemetry-phase1-evidence.v1.json)
binds its measured clean source revision, the complete proof-source byte
closure, and the exact receipt bytes; the recurring local proof reopens it
before running the smoke profile.

This is the Phase-1 surface from
[LLP 0154](repo:llp/0154-minimal-observability.rfc.md): backend requests,
function and job runs, live/WebSocket lifecycle, process and release markers,
runtime logs, and standalone diagnostics. It does not include hosted telemetry,
declared product-analytics events, distinct-user metrics, funnels, or client
crash ingest. Grouped backend issue lifecycle is the separate
[error-tracking capability](./error-tracking.md) built on these rows.

## Check health and recent logs in the console

Open the admin console and select **Health** for request volume, request error
rate, p50/p95 latency, live connections, top routes/functions, lifecycle
markers, and drop counters. Select **Logs** to filter raw events by kind, name,
diagnostic code, or text and inspect one record.

Health reads the closed aggregate `telemetry.stats` projection. Logs reads
`telemetry.events`, whose records can contain authored log text or diagnostic
context and therefore require the separate scoped secret-read authority. The
console acquires that authority through its existing operator boundary; an app
session never grants it.

## Query the typed operations from the CLI

Address the server by its readiness descriptor so the CLI can resolve its URL,
admin credential, and—only for raw reads—a short-lived scoped lease:

```sh
snapback telemetry stats --ready-file .snapback/server-ready.json --kind function_run
snapback telemetry events --ready-file .snapback/server-ready.json --kind log --limit 50 --order desc
snapback telemetry export --ready-file .snapback/server-ready.json --since 1760000000000 --until 1760086400000 > telemetry.ndjson
```

`stats` admits `--kind`, `--name`, `--from-ms`/`--since`, and
`--to-ms`/`--until`. `events` and `export` additionally admit `--status`,
`--code`, `--correlation`, and `--text`; `events` has the deterministic
`recorded_ts_ms` + `id` cursor and a page limit of 1–500. Export freezes one
snapshot and emits a self-describing NDJSON header followed by the visible
records.

When addressing `--url` instead, supply the admin token and a separately
minted `--secret-read-lease` for `events` or `export`. An admin token alone is
deliberately insufficient for raw records. Responses from raw HTTP carriers
are `no-store`.

## Query from an agent tool

The control MCP exposes the same Rust-owned operations as:

- `snapback_telemetry_stats` — aggregate counts, error rates, latency,
  coverage, and variance;
- `snapback_telemetry_events` — one bounded raw-event page with an
  automatically minted scoped lease;
- `snapback_telemetry_export` — one immutable-snapshot page bounded by
  `maxRows` and `maxBytes`, plus an opaque continuation token when truncated.

The host-operation identities are `telemetry.stats`, `telemetry.events`, and
`telemetry.export`. The agent export is intentionally finite; follow its
continuation token rather than treating one page as the whole snapshot.

## Read the variance envelope before drawing conclusions

Every typed response reports its store backend, capability outcome, sampling,
freshness watermark, retention boundary, truncation, and drop counters.
Window totals are exact only when the reported coverage spans the requested
window. Per-name results become approximate when heavy-hitter folding occurred;
latency percentiles are histogram approximations with stated bounds.

Telemetry may shed under pressure. Since-boot and lifetime counters say what
was lost and why. A missing event after a nonzero drop count is not evidence
that the operation never happened, and an old freshness watermark is not a
current health reading. Telemetry is never billing authority.

## Use the local SQL hatch for bounded investigations

When the typed operations cannot express a local investigation, query the app
database's telemetry sibling through the CLI:

```sh
snapback telemetry query \
  "SELECT kind, name, count(*) AS n FROM telemetry_events_visible GROUP BY kind, name" \
  --db .snapback/dev.sqlite3 --max-rows 100 --max-time-ms 2000
```

The command opens `.snapback/dev.sqlite3.telemetry` read-only and permits one
statement over `telemetry_events_visible` or `telemetry_rollup_visible`.
Base-table reads, writes, pragmas, attach/detach, extension loading, and SQL
tails are refused. Row, SQLite-step, elapsed-time, and serialized-byte budgets
remain enforced even though the command is local. There is no network SQL
endpoint.

## Understand storage and retention

Telemetry uses its own generation-bound SQLite sibling and write connection;
it is not attached to the app database, does not enter application tables or
live-query changes, and rotates visibility with reset/restore incarnation.
Producers enqueue without waiting for SQLite. A record arrival arms a flush at
256 records or when the oldest record reaches 3 seconds; retention, rollups,
checkpointing, and generation cleanup ride that flush path rather than a
periodic timer.

The local defaults retain 7 days of raw events, reserve 512 of 4,096 buffer
slots for failure/terminal records, and cap the physical telemetry main + WAL
+ SHM footprint at 256 MiB. These are deployment-owned resource-safety
settings, not plan entitlements. `maxDays: 0` is a true persistence off switch.
Automation should inspect the returned retention/variance facts instead of
assuming defaults; the current author-facing CLI does not mutate this policy.

## Anti-patterns

- **Do not use telemetry to compute bills, audit ledgers, or durable app
  state.** It is explicitly loss-tolerant and priority-shedding.
- **Do not treat the admin token as raw-data authority.** Events and exports
  require their own short-lived, budgeted secret-read scope.
- **Do not open telemetry base tables or hand-edit the config sibling.** Use
  typed operations, or the bounded local visibility-view hatch.
- **Do not infer zero activity from an empty page without checking freshness,
  coverage, retention, truncation, and drops.**
- **Do not build product analytics or a second error-group lifecycle on raw
  Phase-1 rows.** Product analytics remains unbuilt; use the typed
  [error-tracking capability](./error-tracking.md) for backend issue triage.

# Backend error tracking

> **Local target only.** This page describes the local dev/test target.
> Hosted targets make deliberately weaker or different claims — see
> [auth/targets](../auth/targets.md).

Snapback groups eligible backend failures into durable-within-retention
issues, keeps occurrence and suppression counts, and remembers whether each
issue is open, resolved, ignored, or regressed. Start with the fixed Errors
console page for triage. Use the typed operations when an agent needs exact
filters, raw exemplars, or compare-and-swap state transitions.

This is LLP 0156's local Phase E0/E1 capability, built on the
[observability substrate](./observability.md). It is partial rather than a
general crash service: grouped state does not ship on the Cloudflare target;
E2 alert delivery is unbuilt; and E3 client crash ingest is unbuilt.
Server-side stacks are raw rather than symbolicated.

When one handler terminal contains multiple ordered unhandled rejections, it
remains one observation. The first ordered rejection supplies the exception
class and normalized message template for one fingerprint and one exemplar;
the terminal increments that group's occurrence count once. The complete
ordered carrier vector remains in the raw telemetry event's
`details.rejectionCarriers` facts, within the ordinary bounded-details and
truncation rules. Snapback neither creates one group per rejection nor invents
an aggregate fingerprint.

## Triage open and regressed issues in the console

Open the admin console and select **Errors**. The list combines open and
regressed issues in last-seen order, with occurrence, release, and suppression
counts. Resolve or ignore an issue from its row. Each action sends the row's
current `stateSeq`, so another actor's intervening transition produces a
visible conflict instead of overwriting it.

Raw templates and stack heads are absent from list rows. Select the explicit
detail action to acquire the scoped raw-read lease and load one issue's
retained exemplars. Normal console bootstrap and Health polling never load raw
detail. Health's Errors tile is only a link-out count derived from the same
structural issue reads; it is not a second query path.

## Ask the release-first questions from the CLI

Address the server by its readiness descriptor so the CLI can resolve the
server, admin credential, and—only for raw issue detail—the short-lived scoped
lease:

```sh
snapback errors issues --ready-file .snapback/server-ready.json
snapback errors issues --ready-file .snapback/server-ready.json --since release-a --state regressed
snapback errors issue iss_00000000000000000000000000 --ready-file .snapback/server-ready.json
```

`errors issues` defaults `since` to the newest retained release. Supply
`--state`, `--kind`, `--name`, `--subsystem`, `--failure-disposition`,
`--release`, `--since`, `--from-ms`, `--to-ms`, `--order last-seen|count`,
`--cursor`, or `--limit` to narrow the structural list. An unknown release, or
one older than the visible activation floor, fails closed and reports the
known retained releases.

`errors issue <iss_…>` returns one structural issue plus retained template and
stack-head exemplars, bounded transition history, and a ready-to-run
`telemetry.events` correlation query per exemplar. With `--url` instead of a
readiness file, provide both the admin token and a separately minted
`--secret-read-lease`; an admin token alone cannot read raw detail.

## Transition state without losing a concurrent update

Read the issue's current `stateSeq`, then supply it as the CAS expectation:

```sh
snapback errors transition iss_00000000000000000000000000 \
  --ready-file .snapback/server-ready.json --to resolved --expect-seq 3
```

The authored targets are `open`, `resolved`, and `ignored`; `regressed` is a
flusher-authored state when a new eligible occurrence is accepted after the
resolve barrier. A stale `expectSeq` returns a conflict with no transition.
Transition history is bounded, so use the group row's current state and
`stateSeq` as authority and read the reported history floor before treating
the visible history as complete.

For a deploy hook, resolve all open or regressed issues last seen before one
retained release activation:

```sh
snapback errors resolve --ready-file .snapback/server-ready.json --open-before release-a
```

The selector and transitions execute in one telemetry-store transaction. The
response reports an applied, skipped, missing, or conflict outcome per issue;
the command does not pretend every selected row was transitionable.

## Use the same operations from an agent tool

The control MCP projects the Rust-owned contract without another issue model:

- `snapback_errors_issues` projects `errors.issues`, the structural list;
- `snapback_errors_issue` projects `errors.issue` and automatically mints the
  bounded `errors-issue` secret-read lease; and
- `snapback_errors_transition` projects either the single CAS form or the
  atomic `openBefore` bulk-resolve form.

List and detail operations report the observability variance envelope plus
error-group facts. Check `groupHorizonStartMs` before assuming an old resolved
issue would still be remembered; `transitionHistoryFloorSeq` and
`transitionHistoryTruncated` before treating history as complete;
`exemplarStale` and exemplar drop counters before assuming raw detail never
existed; and `overflowFoldCount` before treating the visible groups as every
eligible fingerprint. Suppression counts record rollout/cooldown decisions;
they do not imply an alert was delivered, because E2 delivery is not built.

## Understand what survives and what does not

Issue groups, transitions, activations, and raw exemplars live in the same
generation-bound telemetry sibling database. The classification group can
outlive its raw exemplar, but deleting the telemetry file, rotating the app
generation, reaching the group horizon, or setting `maxDays: 0` removes it
from the visible issue surface. This is triage state, not an audit ledger.

Declared application refusals are issue-eligible only when the function
explicitly lists the admitted code in `trackedRefusals`. The private opt-in is
validated as a subset of `refusals` and is never added to public function
introspection. Ordinary caller errors and untracked app refusals remain out of
the issue list; tracking every failed request would erase the distinction
between actionable faults and routine domain outcomes.

## Anti-patterns

- **Do not query `error_groups` directly or build a second grouping store.**
  Use `errors.*`; grouping and raw telemetry share one flush transaction and
  one generation fence.
- **Do not put stack or template text on a structural list or webhook.** Raw
  content requires the scoped detail lease and must remain `no-store` on HTTP.
- **Do not update state without `stateSeq`.** A timestamp is informational;
  the sequence is the concurrency token.
- **Do not infer alert delivery from suppression counters.** E2's outbox,
  retries, webhook, and Sentry-formatted bridge are deferred and unbuilt.
- **Do not send browser or native crashes to the backend issue routes.** E3's
  authority, abuse limits, offline ordering, protocol, and symbolication are
  deferred to a separate RFC and are unbuilt.

# Client protocol

> **Local target only.** This page describes the local dev/test target.
> Hosted targets make deliberately weaker or different claims — see
> [auth/targets](../auth/targets.md).

Use this page when a platform cannot run `@expo/snapback-client`. The committed JSON
Schemas are the exact wire shapes; the
[`snapback.v1` fixture corpus](repo:schemas/live.wire-fixtures.v1.json) is the
language-neutral conformance entry point. The protocol does not make a client
safe by itself: lifecycle, demand release, auth invalidation, and retries are
part of conformance.

## Choose a delivery lane

- `poll/local`: open a connection, subscribe, and drain
  `GET /outbox/{connectionId}` on one non-overlapping declared cadence.
- `live/local`: open a connection, subscribe, and attach
  `GET /live/{connectionId}/stream` as a WebSocket.
- `live/hosted`: specified, but each hosted target must prove it separately.
- `poll/hosted`: not claimable. Hosted demand is socket-owned today.

Both local lanes begin with `POST /connection/open`. Offer
`wireVersion: "snapback.v1"` and carry the returned connection token on every
connection-scoped request. A WebSocket offers `snapback.v1` plus
`snapback.connection-token.<token>` as subprotocols.

`@expo/snapback-client` verifies the open response echoes that exact version. Its
compatibility bridge downgrades only when the exact pre-B1 decode refusal
disappears on one offerless retry, or when an offered hosted open succeeds
without the B1 echo; either case emits a structured diagnostic and is cached
per endpoint. Set `strictWireVersion: true` to refuse any unproven legacy
binding instead of using the bridge.

## Keep the envelope families distinct

The casing differences are wire contract, not style:

| Family | Where | Tag and casing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `LiveEnvelope` | durable updates | `kind`, mostly `snake_case` |
| `LiveSocketServerFrame` | socket control | `kind`, mostly `camelCase` members |
| `RealtimeEnvelope` | HTTP drain wrapper | externally tagged `Durable` / `Ephemeral` |

Socket durable frames are unwrapped. HTTP drain durable frames are byte payloads
inside `{"Durable": {"payload": [...]}}`; decode the bytes, then dispatch the
inner `LiveEnvelope`. Unknown kinds and unknown fields are skipped. A known kind
missing required fields after the drain ownership cut is data loss and forces
connection-wide resync.

## Apply versions and recover deliberately

Track the last applied version per subscription. Drop an ordinary
`live_replace`, `live_delta`, or `current_as_of` whose version is not newer.
Apply delta operations by row id. `resync_required` re-enters the named
subscription through fresh snapshot-with-subscribe; an absent subscription id
means every subscription and retained ephemeral overlay must resync.

The socket has an application heartbeat: send `{"type":"ping"}` every five
seconds and require a `pong` or other activity inside the 15-second freshness
budget. A missed budget forces socket loss and reconnect. Reconnect is always a
fresh subscribe with `supersedes`; it is not implicit resume.

On mobile, do not infer death from a quiet socket. Backgrounding explicitly
releases demand and quiesces transport. Foregrounding reconnects and performs
fresh snapshot-with-subscribe. The
[Swift client](../clients/swift.md) exposes this as
`pauseForBackground()` / `resumeAfterForeground()`; JS live-query handles use
`pause()` / `resume()`.

## Offer session auth exactly

A client holding a Snapback session bearer repeats
`x-snapback-auth-client-protocol: 1` on authenticated request/response work.
This includes `POST /connection/open`: the route is Public for credential
classification, but sessions mode still applies the `auth/rr` capability gate.
Auth-scoped live additionally requires:

1. `authInvalidationProtocol: 1` in `POST /connection/open`;
2. `x-snapback-auth-invalidation-protocol: 1` on every live subscribe and
   unsubscribe (a client cannot infer target independence);
3. a stable `authorizationNamespace` with `clientStoreId`, `queryKey`, and
   positive `queryInstanceId`; and
4. handling `authorization_invalidation` as the primary row-delivery lane.

Apply the invalidation frame's camelCase `snapshot` atomically, then POST
`{connectionId, ackToken}` to
`/live/authorization-invalidation/acknowledge`. Never acknowledge a snapshot
that was not applied. A duplicate redelivery whose version is already held is
safe to acknowledge again; do not regress rows.

Session mode rejects client-selected identity in bodies. Carry the bearer in
`Authorization`; omit `auth.user_id`.

After connection open, connection-scoped HTTP and WebSocket routes authenticate
the returned connection grant and ignore a session bearer. A changed identity
therefore opens a fresh grant and establishes fresh subscriptions; replacing a
bearer on an old connection cannot change its bound authority.

## Bind generated calls to one sessions generation

When a client consumes a complete generated sessions pair, copy its exact
`expectedGeneration` object onto query, mutation, action, authorized-lease, and
live-subscribe bodies. The five required strings are `schemaVersion`, `appId`,
`schemaHash`, `bundleHash`, and `inputsHash`. A mismatch is HTTP 409
`SNAPBACK_ARTIFACT_IDENTITY_MISMATCH` with
`details.subcause: "generation"`; refetch the artifacts and retry as a new
operation. Successful sessions answers echo server-derived
`facts.activeGeneration`.

Subscriptions pin the assertion. On activation, handle
`resync_required.reason === "SNAPBACK_ARTIFACT_IDENTITY_MISMATCH"` as a request
to discard predecessor rows and establish from refreshed artifacts. A removed
function remains `SNAPBACK_UNKNOWN_FUNCTION`, not a generation mismatch.

The field is additive. Omit it when the caller has no complete generated pair;
the server deliberately leaves that legacy call unchecked. Dev accepts the
field without enforcing it and does not echo sessions generation facts.

## Release demand

Normal shutdown and backgrounding unsubscribe explicitly. Socket close releases
server demand, and the local idle reaper is a crash backstop, not a lifecycle
API. There is exactly one drain owner per connection.

## Anti-patterns

- Do not normalize the mixed casing.
- Do not pass bearer or connection tokens in URLs.
- Do not treat a quiet socket as dead without heartbeat evidence.
- Do not handle only `live_replace`; auth-scoped rows arrive through
  `authorization_invalidation`.
- Do not claim a lane/target tuple that the fixture corpus and a live witness
  did not prove.

# Live queries

> **Local target only.** This page describes the local dev/test target.
> Hosted targets make deliberately weaker or different claims — see
> [auth/targets](../auth/targets.md).

A live query is an ordinary query definition that clients can subscribe
to: subscribers get an authoritative initial snapshot **with** the
subscription (never a prime race), then server-pushed updates over the
durable lane as commits change the result.

## Define one

Mark the definition live — declarative or JS style
([your first backend](../getting-started/your-first-backend.md) covers the
two styles):

```js source=demos/todo/snapback/functions.mjs
export const listTodos = defineJsLiveQuery({
  args: {},
  source: 'handlers.mjs',
  exportName: 'listTodos',
  reads: ['todos'],
  authScopeField: 'userId',
```

`defineLiveQuery` is the declarative twin (same spec as `defineQuery` plus
`defaultLive: false` to make live opt-in per subscription). `reads:` and
`authScopeField:` matter: they drive invalidation and per-principal scoping
(see [auth](../auth/sessions-and-principals.md)). Subscribing to a non-live
function fails with `SNAPBACK_FUNCTION_NOT_LIVE`.

Offline cold retention is a separate per-query opt-in: `auth: 'public'` +
`authorityIndependent: true` on a declarative live query makes it
`rqsEligible`; without the declaration nothing persists and the handle's
`retention` fact names the refusal. The full recipe is in
[offline retention](../sync/offline-and-retention.md).

Stored document contracts include typed `v.assetRef` fields. A photo-bearing
table can therefore be queried directly as a live feed; the reference arrives
as its opaque asset-id string. Keep the typed reference on the row that owns
its sharing and GC semantics instead of maintaining a second string copy or a
side table for live delivery (see [Assets](../backend/assets.md#put-typed-photos-directly-in-a-live-feed)).

## Subscribe

`client.liveQuery(ref, options)` returns a handle with the snapshot already
applied — `rows`, `connection`, `poll()`, `dispose()`:

```js source=demos/todo/tests/acceptance/headless.mjs
    const handle = await db.liveQuery(api.listTodos, { connectionId: 'client_a', userId: ADA });
    assertEqual(handle.rows.length, 3, 'snapshot rows');
```

Cross-client delivery is the point — one client mutates, the other's
subscription updates:

```js source=demos/todo/tests/acceptance/headless.mjs
    const b = await db.liveQuery(api.listTodos, { connectionId: 'client_b', userId: ADA });
    assertEqual(b.rows.length, 3, 'b initial');
    await db.mutate(api.createTodo, { args: { title: 'Added by another client' }, userId: ADA });
    const rows = await b.poll();
    assertEqual(rows.length, 4, 'b did not receive realtime update');
```

Key options: `transport: 'stream'` for durable WebSocket push (`'poll'` is
the default, cadence `pollCadenceMs`, with `fallbackToPoll` when a stream
can't be established), `onUpdate(rows, meta)`, `onConnectionChange`,
`connectionId` (one shared socket per connection id multiplexes all of that
connection's live handles), and per-socket `stream:` tuning
(heartbeat/freshness/reconnect). Always `dispose()` handles you created.
The supplied `connectionId` is a readable client-local label; the kit resolves
and refreshes its opaque granted wire id for high-level calls. A low-level
adapter constructing raw frames must use
`(await client.connectionGrant(label)).id`, never the readable label.

## Logical keyed bindings

One physical handle is not necessarily one component binding. The dynamic
Contract provider lets Exact key a logical attempt by opaque authority
partition, stable descriptor identity and compatibility token, and canonical
arguments. Same-key siblings share data/error/reconnect state but dispose by
independent refcount; different args, descriptors, providers, or authority
partitions stay isolated. An authority change clears predecessor rows before
reopening, so a late result cannot cross the privacy cut.

This layer is for generated/framework integrations. Direct headless callers
still own each `client.liveQuery()` handle they create. See
[the Contract adapter](../clients/contract-adapter.md) for the shipped dynamic
mode and its current live-push/no-offline profile boundary.

## What arrives: replace and delta

Durable updates carry a `meta.kind`: `live_replace` (a full snapshot of the
result) or `live_delta` (incremental add/remove — the analyzable
unordered/filtered subset gets deltas; ordered queries fall back to
replace; LLP 0008 §DK-3). `resync_required` tells the client to
re-snapshot; `authorization_invalidation` is the auth barrier
([protecting data](../auth/protecting-data.md)). Auth-scoped
subscriptions — anything gated by a membership predicate or another
protected-query input — deliver through the witnessed lane instead of
the plain kinds: expect `authorization_snapshot` (an auth-verified
result snapshot) and `authorization_quarantine` (the result blanked at
a governed boundary, e.g. when the caller leaves the membership). A
membership-gated feed never sees a bare `live_replace`; handle all
four kinds. A subscription
asserts on delta kinds like this:

Incremental publication also requires the query's exact, schema-derived
`Documents` result contract. A `live_delta` publishes committed storage rows
without rerunning the complete query, so a `Documents` tag, table name, or
hand-written narrower descriptor is not enough to prove that those rows match
the operation's egress contract. Codegen supplies the exact contract and hash
for an ordinary authored declarative query. Internal fixtures that construct a
function manifest directly must derive the contract through the same codegen
path, as the linked executable fixture does; do not invent a descriptor by
hand. A missing or non-exact contract does not make the live query unloadable:
the server honestly takes the full re-query plus `live_replace` path instead.

When an apparently analyzable query receives replacements, check all of the
conservative boundaries together: ordered or limited queries, membership-gated
queries, generated standard patterns, opaque handlers, and manifests without
the exact schema-derived document contract are replace-only. This fallback is
intentional and correctness-preserving, not evidence that durable push failed.

```js source=demos/_kit/tests/live-delta-e2e.mjs
  const handle = await db.liveQuery('listMine', {
    connectionId: 'delta_conn',
    userId: ADA,
    transport: 'stream',
    stream: { heartbeatIntervalMs: 200, freshnessBudgetMs: 800, reconnectBaseDelayMs: 100, reconnectMaxDelayMs: 400 },
    onUpdate: rec.onUpdate,
  });
```

Membership-gated live replacement does not make a query safe for offline
retention. V1 refuses retained role-gated queries until an authorized lease can
bind the exact membership declaration/resource dependency and expiry floor.
For online live state, declaration-bound `requireRole` dependencies are
revocation-active: resource- or app-scoped membership deletion/downgrade first
blanks the established result, then a trusted denial terminally deletes it and
ACKs the exact obligation. Fresh reads remain denied and later writes cannot
repopulate that handle.

## Connection state an author can observe

The stream manager emits `'connecting'`, `'open'`, `'lost'`
(`{ wasOpen }`), `'budget-missed'` (socket claims open but the freshness
budget lapsed), and `'closed'`. The kit derives a per-query `connection`
axis from these and pushes it through `onConnectionChange`; the conventional
author-facing mapping (from the cursors-web hook) is:

```ts source=demos/cursors-web/surfaces/react/src/useCursorRoom.ts
export type ConnectionAxis = 'connecting' | 'live' | 'stale' | 'disconnected';
```

`open → live`; `budget-missed`/`lost → stale` (degraded — render retained
data, marked); `closed → disconnected`. Defaults:
`LIVE_HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL_MS = 5_000`, `LIVE_FRESHNESS_BUDGET_MS = 15_000`,
reconnect backoff 250ms → 10s. The
[headless client](../clients/headless.md) owns this state machine; the
[Contract adapter](../clients/contract-adapter.md) and React arm consume it.

## Anti-patterns

- **Do not poll a query you can subscribe to.** `liveQuery` exists;
  hand-rolled `setInterval` re-query loops re-derive a worse version of the
  poll transport and never get durable push.
- **Do not treat a socket as fresh because it is open.** `budget-missed`
  exists precisely because "open" and "fresh" diverge; consume the
  connection axis, not `isOpen()`.
- **Do not leak handles.** Every `liveQuery`/overlay handle is `dispose()`d
  in teardown (React: effect cleanup; suites: `cleanups`).
- **Do not combine component-local state or counter deltas with a value a
  live query already delivers.** Viewer-specific facts (a `liked` flag, a
  count) belong in the query result; zero-latency interaction comes from an
  optimistic projection over that same store, which reconciles with later
  authoritative deliveries instead of double-applying — see
  [the optimistic toggle recipe](../recipes/optimistic-toggle.md).

# Ephemeral realtime state

> **Local target only.** This page describes the process-local dev/test
> target. A hosted target needs sticky room routing or a shared room adapter;
> Snapback does not currently claim that hosted capability.

Ephemeral collections are typed, authorized, TTL-bounded latest-state maps for
presence, cursors, selections, typing, drag state, and live viewport state.
They are deliberately lossy: if a value must survive restart, support offline
reads, or enter history/audit, put it in a durable table instead.

Start with the [presence-cursors recipe](../recipes/presence-cursors.md) when
building a feature. Use this page when choosing collection options or handling
recovery.

## Declare the complete collection contract

One collection declaration contains every routing, ownership, budget,
delivery, validation, and access fact:

```js source=demos/cursors-web/snapback/schema.mjs
    webCursors: ephemeral.collection({
      scope: { roomId: v.string() },
      routing: ['roomId'],
      key: 'connection',
      ttlMs: 5_000,
      maxTtlMs: 30_000,
      maxValueBytes: 1_024,
      publishRate: { sustainedHz: 20, burst: 40 },
      delivery: { mode: 'latest', dispatchMs: 33 },
      value: v.object({
        x: v.number(),
        y: v.number(),
        name: v.string(),
        color: v.string(),
        updatedAt: v.optional(v.number()),
      }),
      publish: allow.all(),
      subscribe: allow.all(),
    }),
```

The option inventory is:

| Option | Local contract |
| --- | --- |
| `scope` | Required non-empty validator object. Its normalized values partition snapshots, fan-out, and authorization. |
| `routing` | Defaults to every scope field; must be a non-empty, duplicate-free subset of `scope`. |
| `key` | `connection` by default; also `session`, `user`, or `custom`. |
| `ttlMs` | Required positive default lease. There is no immortal entry. |
| `maxTtlMs` | Defaults to and may not exceed 30,000ms; must be at least `ttlMs`. |
| `maxValueBytes` / `hardMaxValueBytes` | Defaults 1,024/4,096 bytes; neither may cross the 4 KiB local hard cap. |
| `publishRate` | Defaults to `{ sustainedHz: 20, burst: 60 }`, enforced per connection/collection. |
| `delivery` | Defaults to `{ mode: 'latest', dispatchMs: 33 }`; `latest` is the only shipped mode. |
| `publish` / `subscribe` | Both required explicit policies: `allow.all()` or `allow.roomPermission(prefix)`. |
| `value` | Required portable validator; generated clients and the server validate it. |
| `targets` | Defaults to `local-dev-sqlite-ibex`; codegen rejects an undeclared selected target. |
| `maxPendingEphemeralKeys` | Defaults to 1,024, bounding coalesced keys retained for dispatch. |

Codegen rejects unsafe routing, absent TTL/auth, unsupported modes/targets,
invalid validators, and over-budget declarations before it writes artifacts.
Do not treat authoring defaults as hosted scale promises.

## Choose a key mode deliberately

- `connection` gives each active connection its own value and reclaims it on
  disconnect or expiry. Its key is the opaque id granted to the transport,
  not the app's readable connection label. It is the normal cursor/presence
  choice.
- `session` derives the key from the authenticated session, so reconnecting
  can refresh the same lease. A caller-supplied session id is only an
  assertion and must match transport authority.
- `user` derives the key from the authenticated user. Multiple connections
  refresh one shared lease; use it only when presence privacy permits.
- `custom` accepts several connection-owned keys. Until generated
  key-specific authorization exists, only the creating connection may replace
  or delete each key.

Never put a display name or caller-asserted user id in charge of ownership.
The transport-derived connection/session/user identity is authoritative.

## Authorize publish and subscribe separately

`allow.all()` is explicit public room access. For protected rooms, use the
same room permission prefix on publish and subscribe and grant the normalized
permission through the connection authority:

```js fragment reason="Policy fragment; protected room fixture uses a different domain-specific prefix."
publish: allow.roomPermission('boardPresence'),
subscribe: allow.roomPermission('boardPresence'),
```

The matching permission string is
`SnapbackClient.roomPermission('boardPresence', scope)`. A room protected by
durable membership also participates in the authorization-invalidation
barrier. Membership-backed room authority binds to the declaration's stable id,
not a table name or ambient role string; removing or downgrading a required role
quiesces affected room sinks before the commit becomes visible. Custom-key
authorization beyond connection ownership is not shipped.

## Subscribe to snapshot plus deltas

`subscribeEphemeral(ref, { connectionId, scope, ... })` registers the lane
consumer before requesting its authoritative snapshot, buffers in-flight
deltas, then applies them after the snapshot boundary. Its default
`transport: "stream"` path acquires managed-socket demand and proves current
ping/pong readiness itself before subscribing; a fresh connection label needs
no prior durable query and no manual
`liveStreamManager(connectionId).waitUntilReady()` call. The overlay owns that
demand until `dispose()`. Use `transport: "poll"` only for an explicit
headless/manual-drain consumer.

The returned overlay
provides `currentEntries()`, `onChange`, `publish`, `delete`, `drain`, and
`dispose`, plus `grantedConnectionId`: the exact opaque connection id used by
that successful subscribe. Compare a connection-owned entry's `key` with this
field to identify self. Do not compare it with the readable `connectionId`
argument, which only keys the client's grant/socket registries and may diverge
after collision or mint-only containment.

Each current entry is:

```text fragment reason="Normalized public entry shape assembled by EphemeralOverlay.currentEntries()."
{ key, value, expiresAtMs, receivedAtMs, scopeEpoch, entryVersion }
```

The client prunes by the server-stamped expiry deadline. Server expiry,
explicit delete, and disconnect normally emit remove deltas, but TTL is the
backstop when that remove is lost.

## Treat epochs and versions as one-room coordinates

`entryVersion` is a monotonic room-local high-water coordinate, meaningful
only for one collection/scope and within one `scopeEpoch`. The overlay ignores
stale versions and keeps bounded tombstones so an old upsert cannot resurrect
a removed entry.

An epoch mismatch, queue overflow, or connection-wide continuity loss produces
the level-triggered `needs_resync` state. Blank/degrade the UI, create a fresh
overlay with `subscribeEphemeral`, attach its listener, then dispose the old
overlay. Do not compare ephemeral versions with durable commit versions, and
do not reopen a connection-poisoned overlay with a delayed snapshot.

## Use generated Contract links

Codegen emits a typed `*.ephemeral.ts` read descriptor, a
`*.publish.ts` descriptor, their Contract metadata, and runtime links. A
Contract component reads the map as an `ephemeral` binding:

```contract source=demos/cursors-web/surfaces/contract/app.contract
  ephemeral cursors = webCursors({ roomId: "lobby" })
```

The surface prewarms the room and configures the generated links; authored
`publish ... rate=N` channels are statically checked against the generated
publish budget. Generated result rows preserve the collection's schema-known
value type; a typed value must not degrade to `unknown` at provider
introspection. Keep imperative overlays in headless/React code and generated
ephemeral links in Contract code—do not mix a second polling or publish lane
into the same surface.

## Anti-patterns

- **Do not store transient motion in tables.** Durable commits and history are
  the wrong correctness model for cursor samples.
- **Do not invent global/unscoped rooms.** Scope is the fan-out and
  authorization boundary.
- **Do not retry rate-limit failures blindly.** Lower the publisher rate and
  observe rejections.
- **Do not trust deltas after `needs_resync`.** Establish a fresh snapshot
  boundary.
- **Do not claim multi-instance presence.** The current shipped adapter is
  process-local.
- **Do not derive self from a readable connection label.** The granted id on
  the overlay is the connection-owned lease key.

examples: [demos/public-dashboard]
status: current
targets: [local, cloudflare]

reviewed: 2026-08-04

# Route snapshot bundles

A snapshot bundle evaluates every query declared for one route at a single
commit cut. Use it to boot a deep-linked page without issuing unrelated query
requests that can observe different database versions. Eligible entries also
carry resumable-query tokens.

The local target supports read and authenticated register mode. The Cloudflare
target supports read-mode bundles and token resume; register mode remains
deferred there.

For a qualifying public authority-independent single-table live query, the
local target now uses the host-derived experimental `single_table_v1@1` class
and QMK identity. Existing legacy RQS entries do not change identity merely
because this class is active: LLP 0090 grandfathers them until a connected
prove-or-fresh adoption installs the QMK record and switches custody in one
atomic same-domain transaction. Adoption never relabels old bytes in place and
never drops pending outbox intent.

### Mix live and read-only children without losing the live siblings

On the contributor local target, a route containing at least one generated
`LiveQuery` and one generated `Query` receives a separate format-2 generated
group with profile `mixed-route.v2`. Preparing that group still evaluates
every child at one `commitVersion`. Only the `LiveQuery` children acquire
subscriptions; ordinary `Query` children return an explicit
`delivery.kind: "read-only"`, keep snapshot freshness, and never open a later
ordinary subscription.

The generated reference carries the LLP 0157 plan and per-child node hashes.
The server rebuilds them from the served manifests before execution. A query's
plan shape never makes it live: changing only its declaration from `Query` to
`LiveQuery` changes the identity-bound capability and therefore rotates the
node and group plan hashes.

Mixed responses are wire `formatVersion: 2`, repeat
`profile: "mixed-route.v2"` and `planHash`, and report a weakest aggregate of
`read-only`. This is intentionally separate from the existing all-live
format-1 group. Capability `mixed_bundle_boot_v2` is Experimental and local-
only; a target without it refuses mixed-group preparation because an ordinary
`Query` cannot honestly be upgraded into a live fallback.

## Declare the route and its query arguments

Routes are generated artifacts. Bind URL parameters through `routeParam`
instead of accepting an ad hoc query list from the caller:

```js source=demos/public-dashboard/snapback/routes.mjs
export default defineRoutes([
  {
    route: '/dashboards/:dashboardId',
    queries: [
      {
        function: 'dashboardMetrics',
        args: { dashboardId: routeParam('dashboardId') },
      },
    ],
  },
]);
```

For anonymous Channel A boot, the query must explicitly declare all three
disclosure facts. None is inferred from the route:

```js source=demos/public-dashboard/snapback/functions.mjs
export const dashboardMetrics = defineLiveQuery({
  table: 'metrics',
  args: { dashboardId: v.string() },
  filter: [eq('dashboardId', arg('dashboardId'))],
  order: [asc('label')],
  index: 'by_dashboard',
  auth: 'public',
  authorityIndependent: true,
  publicInline: true,
});
```

Codegen emits `routes.manifest.json`; provision it beside schema and functions
with `ensureApp({ routes })`. A route may name several queries, but every
argument must be a literal or a declared route-parameter binding.

## Fetch one consistent page snapshot

Read mode is socketless and does not create live demand:

```js source=demos/public-dashboard/tests/acceptance/headless.mjs
    bundle = await app.client.fetchBundle({
      route: '/dashboards/:dashboardId',
      params: { dashboardId: 'ops' },
      mode: 'read',
    });
    assertEqual(bundle.entries.length, 1, 'bundle entry count');
    assertEqual(bundle.entries[0].rows.map(({ label }) => label), ['latency_ms', 'uptime_pct'], 'ops rows');
    assert(typeof bundle.entries[0].resume?.token === 'string', 'resume token missing');
```

The response has one shared `commitVersion` and one entry per declared query.
Each entry contains rows and either a verified resume object or `null`,
according to that query's resumable-query eligibility. An undeclared route is
refused with `SNAPBACK_BUNDLE_ROUTE_UNKNOWN`.

## Arm live demand at the same cut

Authenticated local clients may use `mode: 'register'`. The response then
includes a connection grant and live registration for each entry at the same
commit cut. Pass each returned registration to `liveQuery` as
`registeredSubscription`; the client adopts the bundle-owned subscription
without taking a duplicate snapshot.

Anonymous register mode is refused. Retry it in read mode only when a
socketless public snapshot is acceptable. Register mode on Cloudflare is not
currently claimed.

## Anti-patterns

- Do not send a caller-chosen list of function names to `/app/bundle`.
- Do not mark an authenticated or authority-dependent query `publicInline`.
- Do not compare entry versions as though independently fetched queries share
  a commit; use the bundle's `commitVersion`.
- Do not open a second live subscription after register mode; adopt the
  returned registration.
- Do not treat a resume token as application data or decode it.

# Recipe: presence cursors

> **Local target only.** This page describes the local dev/test target.
> Hosted targets make deliberately weaker or different claims — see
> [auth/targets](../auth/targets.md).

"Two users see each other's cursors" is ephemeral state, not app data: it
lives in typed in-memory rooms with TTL expiry and connection-owned
cleanup (LLP 0013) — never in tables, never polled. The working reference
is `demos/cursors-web`. This recipe is the shortest paved implementation;
the [ephemeral-state reference](../realtime/ephemeral-state.md) inventories
every collection option, key mode, recovery rule, and Contract link.

## 1. Declare the ephemeral collection in the schema

An ephemeral collection is declared beside your tables, with its scope
(the room key), keying, TTL, payload budget, and publish rate all typed
and enforced server-side. The shape (this one is todo-v2's presence
collection; cursors-web's `webCursors` follows the same form):

```js source=demos/todo-v2/snapback/schema.mjs
  ephemeral: defineEphemeral({
    todoPresence: ephemeral.collection({
      scope: { listId: v.string() },
      routing: ['listId'],
      key: 'connection',
      ttlMs: 20_000,
      maxTtlMs: 30_000,
      maxValueBytes: 512,
      publishRate: { sustainedHz: 20, burst: 40 },
      delivery: { mode: 'latest', dispatchMs: 33 },
      value: v.object({
        name: v.string(),
        editing: v.optional(v.boolean()),
      }),
      publish: allow.all(),
      subscribe: allow.all(),
```

`key: 'connection'` makes the lease key the publisher's opaque,
server-granted connection id—presence provenance without a spoofable app
field. The readable `connectionId` that app code passes to the kit is only a
local grant/socket label; it may match the lease key after initial dev
adoption, but collision or mint-only containment makes them diverge.
Regenerate after editing (the generated publish descriptor carries the
budget facts your client code should assert against, e.g. cursors-web
checks its declared publish rate fits `sustainedHz` at init).

## 2. Subscribe to the room

`subscribeEphemeral` returns an overlay that applies the authoritative
snapshot, then buffers and applies deltas from the shared live socket
(registered before the snapshot request, so nothing can fall in the gap).
The default call acquires and readiness-proves its managed stream itself; do
not prime it with a durable subscription or call `waitUntilReady()` first:

```ts source=demos/cursors-web/surfaces/react/src/useCursorRoom.ts
    void client
      .subscribeEphemeral(cursorsRef, { connectionId, scope: { roomId } })
      .then((overlay) => {
        if (disposed) {
          // StrictMode double-mount: the first effect's subscribe may resolve
          // after its cleanup ran — never leak that overlay's lane consumer.
          overlay.dispose();
          return;
        }
        overlayRef.current = overlay;
        subscribedRef.current = true;
        offChange = overlay.onChange(handleChange);
        recompute();
      })
```

Read entries with `overlay.currentEntries()` — each is
`{ key, value, expiresAtMs, ... }`; `entry.key ===
overlay.grantedConnectionId` is "self". `grantedConnectionId` is captured
from the exact successful subscribe attempt, including a token-refresh retry.
`onChange` also delivers a level-triggered `'needs_resync'` when
connection continuity is lost (epoch boundary / queue overflow): present
degraded state, then re-enter with a fresh `subscribeEphemeral` and swap
the overlay. `overlay.dispose()` releases the stream demand. Only manual
headless drain loops should opt into `transport: "poll"`.

## 3. Publish samples under the declared budget

```ts source=demos/cursors-web/surfaces/react/src/useCursorRoom.ts
      overlay
        .publish(value, { ttlMs: PRESENCE_TTL_MS })
        .then(() => {
          state.published += 1;
          if (state.establishedAtMs === null) state.establishedAtMs = Date.now();
        })
        .catch(() => {
          state.rejected += 1;
        });
```

The server enforces the schema's rate and payload budgets — count
rejections rather than retrying blindly. Entries expire on the
server-stamped `expiresAtMs`; the reference hook freezes TTL-pruning while
the connection is `stale`/`disconnected` so departed cursors stay
renderable during degradation instead of silently vanishing.

## Anti-patterns

- **Do not store presence in tables.** Cursor positions in app data means
  commits, versions, and history for state that is worthless in ten
  seconds; the ephemeral store exists for exactly this.
- **Do not invent your own presence keys.** `key: 'connection'` gives you
  provenance; a custom name field is spoofable and duplicates on refresh.
- **Do not compare entry keys with the readable connection label.** Compare
  with `overlay.grantedConnectionId`; only the server grant is lease identity.
- **Do not publish above the declared budget** — assert your sample rate
  fits the generated budget facts at init, like the reference hook does.

# Recipe: hidden hands

> **Local target only.** This page describes the local dev/test target.
> Hosted targets make deliberately weaker or different claims — see
> [auth/targets](../auth/targets.md).

Per-principal secrecy over shared data: a card game where every player
queries the same `myHand` function and sees only their own cards — live,
across logout, and honestly offline. The working reference is
`demos/card-game`, and every claim here is asserted by its acceptance
suite (which runs in the local proof).

Prerequisite: sessions-mode auth —
[sessions and principals](../auth/sessions-and-principals.md). For the complete
grant/invalidation/lease contract behind this recipe, use
[protecting data](../auth/protecting-data.md).

## One query, disjoint worlds

Each player signs in (email code → session) and calls the same query with
no owner argument. The query's explicit
`eq('ownerId', authUserId())` predicate compares rows with the
server-derived session principal:

```js source=demos/card-game/snapback/functions.mjs
  filter: [
    eq('ownerId', authUserId()),
    eq('gameId', arg('gameId')),
  ],
```

For JS live queries, `authScopeField` can additionally declare the principal
field to the live matcher; it never substitutes for the ownership predicate.

```js source=demos/card-game/tests/acceptance/authority-scope.mjs
  const [adaResult, graceResult] = await Promise.all([
    ada.client.query('myHand', { args: { gameId } }),
    grace.client.query('myHand', { args: { gameId } }),
  ]);
```

The suite then asserts the two result sets are disjoint — no card leaks
across principals, finite or live.

## Logout blanks yours, only yours

```js source=demos/card-game/tests/acceptance/authority-scope.mjs
  await ada.client.authLogout();
  assert.deepEqual(adaSurface.boundary.current('hand'), []);
  assert.deepEqual(
    graceSurface.boundary.current('hand').map(({ card }) => card),
    ['king-clubs', 'ten-diamonds'],
  );
```

The invalidation barrier is per-principal and immediate on live
boundaries (LLP 0053).

## Offline retention ends at the lease deadline, exactly

With a client store, an authorized retained query survives a cold process
start while the server is down — readable, marked `stale` — until the
signed lease's client deadline, after which store validation deletes the
hidden rows before any fallback could serve them:

```js source=demos/card-game/tests/acceptance/authority-scope.mjs
  const offlineSurface = await trackSurface(coldGraceOptions);
  assert.equal(offlineSurface.retained(), true);
  assert.equal(offlineSurface.connection(), 'stale');
```

```js source=demos/card-game/tests/acceptance/authority-scope.mjs
  const expiredState = await coldGraceStore.snapshot();
  assert.equal(expiredState.retained[retainedQueryKey], undefined);
  assert.equal(expiredState.queryAuthorization[retainedQueryKey]?.lease, null);
```

## Anti-patterns

- **Do not filter secrets client-side.** Sending the whole game state and
  hiding other hands in the UI is not secrecy; the scoping must be the
  server's.
- **Do not cache authorized rows outside the client store.** The store is
  what enforces the lease deadline; a side cache outlives authorization.
- **Do not pass the player as a query argument.** The server derives the
  principal; an owner argument is spoofable and is rejected in sessions
  mode.

# Recipe: optimistic toggle

> **Local target only.** This page describes the local dev/test target.
> Hosted targets make deliberately weaker or different claims — see
> [auth/targets](../auth/targets.md).

A like/favorite button with a count has two honest query layouts. When one
viewer-aware query returns both `liked` and `likeCount`, the heart and count
flip instantly and the authoritative live query settles both without a
flicker or double increment. When cold retention requires a separate public
viewer-fact query, both facts remain query-owned, but the current optimistic
path can move only the count; the heart settles from that second query's live
delivery. The joined layout is the paved implementation of
`useSnapbackMutation`'s two-field optimistic projection
([the React client](../clients/react.md#run-a-mutation)) for the
toggle-plus-counter shape, and its behavioral claims are asserted by
`packages/snapback-react/optimistic.test.mjs` (run by the package's CI test
suite).

The failure this recipe prevents is real and easy to reach: keep the heart in
component state, add a local `+1` to the count, and the live query
independently delivers the authoritative increment — the UI briefly shows a
two-count jump, and a rebase can visibly flip the heart back. Every fact
below exists to make that impossible.

## Model the viewer's fact in query data

The toggle state is per-viewer data, not UI state. It must come from canonical
query data in one of the two layouts below.

### Joined layout: both fields on the rendered row

The query that renders the button returns both fields for the current viewer
— a server-side join against the viewer's like row plus the denormalized count:

```text
timeline(viewer) -> [{ id, body, ..., liked: boolean, likeCount: number }]
```

If `liked` is absent from all query data, there is nothing authoritative to
reconcile against, and component state is the only place left to put it —
which is exactly the anti-pattern. The joined projection sections below assume
this layout.

### Cold-retained public layout: split the viewer fact

`rqsEligible` v1 is a closed single-table plan, so a retainable posts timeline
cannot join in the viewer's like row. It can coexist with a second public
query keyed by an explicit viewer argument: keep `{ ..., likeCount }` in the
posts query, query like rows with `{ handle: viewerHandle }`, and derive the
heart from the second query:

```tsx fragment reason="generated application query types and component props vary by app"
const likeSet = new Set(myLikes.data?.map((like) => like.postId));
const liked = likeSet.has(post._id);
```

The exact retention declaration and its security boundary are in
[retain public viewer facts by argument, not authority](../sync/offline-and-retention.md#retain-public-viewer-facts-by-argument-not-authority).
An argument is caller-controlled and does not enforce privacy, so this layout
is only for public facts. Private viewer data must use server-derived authority
and the Contract arm's `retainable: true`, `AuthorizedLease` path; never
replace `authUserId()` with an argument merely to make a query retainable.

An optimistic layer is validated against the generated result contract of the
one query store it targets. If `liked` is not a field on the posts result,
projecting `{ liked, likeCount }` into a post row is refused before mutation
dispatch with `SNAPBACK_REACT_OPTIMISTIC_INSTALL_FAILED`. Project only the
field that belongs to that row:

```tsx fragment reason="generated application query types and component props vary by app"
optimistic: {
  query: api.timeline,
  args: {},
  ...projectRecordFields(post._id, { likeCount }),
}
```

The count then moves optimistically, while the heart changes when the
authoritative `myLikes` delivery adds or removes the like row. The boolean is
still derived from canonical query data, not component state. A symmetric
instant heart for the like case would require appending a missing row to
`myLikes`; optimistic create has no paved path in v1, so this split layout does
not promise the joined layout's zero-latency heart. Warble implements this
count-only projection; its acceptance suite proves retained rendering plus
exactly-once like settlement.

## Project both fields atomically when they share a row

For the joined layout, declare one optimistic projection beside the mutation
hook. Two rules carry the recipe, and both are visible in the CI-exercised
fixture:

```js source=packages/snapback-react/optimistic.test.mjs
// Capture the intended outcome at admission. The projection is replayed over
// every newer authoritative base during rebase, so it must set the captured
// outcome; toggling or incrementing the incoming row would re-run the user
// action on replay and visibly invert or double-apply it.
const intended = { liked: true, likeCount: 11 };
const optimisticLike = {
  query: timeline,
  args: {},
  update: (posts) => posts.map((post) => post.id === 'p1' ? { ...post, ...intended } : post),
  isAuthoritative: (posts, receipt) => posts.some((post) => post.id === 'p1'
    && post.liked === receipt.liked && post.likeCount === receipt.likeCount),
};
```

- **`update` is a replayable projection, not an action.** The layer is
  recomputed over every newer authoritative base (overlapping attempts,
  interleaved deliveries, rejection rollback). Compute the intended
  `{ liked, likeCount }` once, outside the reducer, and have the reducer
  *set* that outcome. A reducer that toggles (`liked: !row.liked`) or
  increments (`likeCount: row.likeCount + 1`) re-runs the user action on
  every replay and inverts or double-applies it.
- **Change both fields in one projection.** One layer over one store flips
  the heart and moves the count in the same frame. Splitting them (heart in
  component state, count optimistic — or either combined with a local delta)
  reintroduces the double increment.

In application code the same shape reads:

```tsx fragment reason="mutation and query fields come from the generated application API"
const liked = !post.liked;
const likeCount = Math.max(0, post.likeCount + (post.liked ? -1 : 1));
const toggleLike = useSnapbackMutation(api.toggleLike, {
  optimistic: {
    query: api.timeline,
    args: { viewerHandle: viewer },
    update: (posts) => posts.map((item) =>
      item._id === post._id ? { ...item, liked, likeCount } : item),
    isAuthoritative: (posts, receipt) => posts.some((item) =>
      item._id === post._id
        && item.liked === receipt.liked
        && item.likeCount === receipt.likeCount),
  },
});
```

Return the complete receipt — `{ liked, likeCount }` — from the mutation, and
match **both** fields in `isAuthoritative`. A mutation that writes the like
row and the denormalized count separately can produce a live delivery
containing only half the outcome (`liked: true` with the old count). A
matcher that checks only `liked` retires the layer on that partial delivery
and the count visibly dips. Matching the full receipt keeps the layer
installed across partial deliveries — the projection simply rebases over
them:

```js source=packages/snapback-react/optimistic.test.mjs
likeClient.emit('timeline', [{ id: 'p1', liked: true, likeCount: 10 }]);
assert.equal(view().timeline.data[0].liked, true, 'replay does not invert the heart');
assert.equal(view().timeline.data[0].likeCount, 11, 'partial delivery keeps the layer installed');
```

## Or declare it: `projectRecordFields`

Both rules are mechanical, so `@expo/snapback-react` derives them from one
declaration. `projectRecordFields(recordId, fields)` returns a frozen
`{ update, isAuthoritative }` pair — the idempotent capture-and-set
projection and the complete-receipt matcher — to spread into the same
optimistic options:

```js source=packages/snapback-react/optimistic.test.mjs
// One declaration derives the idempotent capture-and-set update and the
// complete-receipt matcher; spread it into the ordinary optimistic options.
const optimisticHelperLike = {
  query: timeline,
  args: {},
  ...projectRecordFields('p2', { liked: true, likeCount: 4 }, { idField: 'id' }),
};
```

The fixture's rows key on `id`; generated application rows carry the default
`_id`, so application code omits the `idField` option. Intended values must
be primitives (`boolean | number | string | null`) — the helper deliberately
expresses only the capture-and-set shape, so it cannot encode the replay
hazard. Prefer it over a hand-written reducer whenever the projection is
"set these fields on this row". In the split cold-retained layout, pass only
`{ likeCount }`; injecting `liked` into the posts row violates that query's
generated result contract.

Hand-written reducers get a development safety net: at admission the
provider replays the just-validated projection through the reducer a second
time, and a reducer that returns a different result over its own output — a
toggle or an increment — logs one
`SNAPBACK_REACT_OPTIMISTIC_REPLAY_DIVERGENT` console warning per
(mutation, query) site, pointing back at this recipe. The advisory is
observational only: it never changes admission, and an explicit production
`NODE_ENV` skips it. (The heuristic is deliberately broad: a reducer that
intentionally appends a row — an optimistic create, which has no paved path
yet — also trips it.)

## Response and query authority can arrive in either order

The mutation's HTTP response and the live query's delivery of the resulting
commit race, and the layer reconciles both orders without double-applying:

- **Response before query:** the validated response settles the mutation
  promise, but a response is not live-query authority. The layer stays
  installed until a live delivery matches the complete receipt, then retires:

```js source=packages/snapback-react/optimistic.test.mjs
likeClient.inspection().attempts[0].resolve({ liked: true, likeCount: 11 });
assert.deepEqual(await like, { liked: true, likeCount: 11 });
assert.equal(view().timeline.data[0].likeCount, 11, 'settled response alone does not retire the layer');
likeClient.emit('timeline', [{ id: 'p1', liked: true, likeCount: 11 }]);
assert.equal(view().timeline.data[0].likeCount, 11);
likeClient.emit('timeline', [{ id: 'p1', liked: true, likeCount: 12 }]);
assert.equal(view().timeline.data[0].likeCount, 12, 'layer retired after the complete receipt');
```

- **Query before response:** the authoritative delivery advances the base
  first and the projection rebases over it (capture-and-set makes this a
  no-op rather than a second increment); when the response then identifies
  the receipt, the matcher recognizes it in the already-current rows and
  retires the layer.

Rejection needs no handling beyond the promise: the layer rolls back
automatically, removing only itself and recomputing anything stacked above it
over the newest authoritative base.

## The same record on multiple surfaces

A post renders in the timeline, on the author's profile, maybe in a detail
view — each a distinct canonical query store. In v1 one optimistic projection
targets exactly one canonical query/args pair: the store that rendered the
component the user touched. Configure the mutation per surface, commonly
through a small surface-specific wrapper around a shared card:

```tsx fragment reason="surface wrappers depend on the application's query surfaces"
export function TimelinePostCard({ post }: { post: Post }) {
  const toggleLike = useToggleLike(post, api.timeline, { viewerHandle: viewer });
  return <PostCard post={post} toggleLike={toggleLike} />;
}

export function ProfilePostCard({ post, handle }: { post: Post; handle: string }) {
  const toggleLike = useToggleLike(post, api.profilePosts, { handle, viewerHandle: viewer });
  return <PostCard post={post} toggleLike={toggleLike} />;
}
```

Only the touched surface gets the zero-latency projection. Every other
mounted store showing the same record updates through its own authoritative
subscription when the commit's live delivery arrives — do not try to install
the same layer into sibling stores or mirror the change into them by hand:

```js source=packages/snapback-react/optimistic.test.mjs
// Other mounted stores rendering the same record update through their own
// authoritative subscriptions, not through the optimistic layer.
likeClient.emit('profilePosts', [{ id: 'p1', liked: true, likeCount: 12 }]);
assert.equal(view().profile.data[0].liked, true, 'other surfaces settle authoritatively');
assert.equal(view().profile.data[0].likeCount, 12);
```

The tradeoff is honest: on the untouched surfaces the like lands at
live-delivery latency rather than instantly. That brief skew is
self-reconciling; a hand-mirrored update is a second source of truth that is
not.

## Anti-patterns

- **Do not add a component-local delta to a count a live query already
  supplies.** `likeCount + localBump` double-counts the moment the
  authoritative increment arrives. The count on screen is either the query's
  value or the optimistic layer's projection of it — never query value plus
  local arithmetic.
- **Do not keep the toggle in component state.** `useState(liked)` has no
  reconciliation with query authority: it drifts on other-client changes,
  survives rejection, and fights the live delivery. Model the fact in query
  data: either as a field on the rendered row or as a boolean derived from a
  separate canonical likes query.
- **Do not project a field into the wrong query's row contract.** In the split
  cold-retained layout, `{ liked, likeCount }` is not a valid posts row when
  `liked` lives in `myLikes`; the layer is refused. Project `{ likeCount }`
  only and let the heart settle from the authoritative viewer-fact query.
- **Do not toggle or increment inside `update`.** The projection is replayed
  during rebase; capture the intended outcome and set it (or let
  `projectRecordFields` do both rules for you). In development the replay
  advisory warns when a reducer diverges over its own output.
- **Do not retire on a partial receipt.** Match every field the mutation
  returns in `isAuthoritative`, or a delivery carrying half the outcome
  retires the layer early and the UI dips.
- **Do not treat the mutation HTTP response as live-query authority.** It
  settles the promise; the layer retires on the matching live delivery.
- **Do not fan one optimistic config out to every store showing the record.**
  v1 targets one canonical query/args pair; sibling surfaces settle through
  their own subscriptions.
- **Do not write a matcher that may never become true.** A layer with an
  `isAuthoritative` never uses the fallback next-delivery retirement: if the
  matched row can be filtered out of the query result, or a matched field
  can settle to a value differing from both receipt and intent, the
  confirmed layer stays installed (and keeps its subscription pin) until the
  store tears down. Match rows the query is guaranteed to keep returning,
  and match fields the mutation actually settles.
